Inverse Text Standardization aims to implement a customizable transformation on text inputs to produce uniform outputs from a given set of text samples. This is crucial for improved performance in text classification, as varying representations of the same text can negatively impact classification accuracy, even necessitating complete model reconstruction. To combat this issue, existing approaches apply a universal standardization, despite this only partially addressing the problem for the smallest text dataset (with fewer than 20 texts). Our proposed solution achieves superior results on this dataset by incorporating multiple data augmentation techniques, ultimately yielding better classification outcomes with reduced variability. This improved outcome also eliminates the need for potential model retraining.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin edge conditions at $x=-\infty$ and 
$x=+\infty$. Additionally, we obtain optimal inequalities for the second eigenvalue 
under these conditions, depending on the sign and magnitude of the Robin coefficient.

This study introduces a novel, highly efficient Bayesian inference technique, 
which leverages low-rank kernel tensors to facilitate nearly exchangeable 
tangential kernel sampling. 
The sampling process in Tk' has a super linear computational cost and 
O(N^2) storage requirement, making it scalable for large datasets. 
We showcase Tk's efficacy through successful integration with l1-minimization 
solutions, presenting fully Bayesian solutions to previously unresolvable 
problems in 1D, that outperform existing methods such as l1-regularized 
nonconvex and weighted l1-sparsity inducing methods, and 
weighted l1-sparsity inducing methods through rigorous comparison. 
A related method, TkL1, was then devised by combining Tk with 
l1-minimization solutions. Notably, TkL1 yields accurate and clean 
solutions prior to convergence of the algorithm. 
A related method, TkL1, was developed by integrating Tk with 
l1-minimization solutions. TkL1 was found to produce reliable and clean 
solutions before its optimization process converges. 
Finally, TkL1 was compared to several other techniques.

Recent discoveries in non-Hermitian non-Hopping systems have shown unique non-Hermitian topological characteristics distinct from their hopping-based counterparts. A notable finding is a broader range of topological classifications and transitions, which often result from extended phase spaces and generalized symmetry protections. A case in point is a one-dimensional non-Hermitian system comprising two distinct forms of interactions: a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetric fermionic interaction and a term causing dissipation. Earlier studies found that system to exhibit unique topological attributes, including $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological classifications and a non-trivial topological structure. However, the current research demonstrates that the $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure in this system is not inherent to non-Hermitian systems, as it can be fully reduced by incorporating hopping terms. A thorough examination of the system's properties using the Hamiltonian analysis reveals the existence of additional topological attributes, such as the $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological structure, which significantly expands the range of non-Hermitian point-gap topology classifications and showcases the complex and nuanced nature of non-Hermitian systems. Moreover, the current research discovers a new class of topological structures in systems without time-reversal symmetry, by designing fermions exhibiting tunable Majorana

This study's primary goal is to examine speaker personality and its relationship to speech content. We sought to achieve this by gathering acoustically relevant personality traits from a crowd-sourced study and developing a training method to incorporate these traits into a limited-liability speech generator. Our results provide an initial understanding of the link between speech characteristics and personality attributes, as well as the potential to create synthetic speech tailored to an individual's personality.

A fundamental approach incorporating a modular $A_4$ symmetry in the standard model with an additional $Z_2$ symmetry is presented, based entirely on high-energy expectations. In this framework, two types of charged fields are allowed, resulting in a rational value for the modular coupling of the right-handed neutrino, while its counterpart for the charged singlet is undetermined. The model predicts the creation of a fully conserved $Z_2$ dark matter particle, produced in equivalent amounts to its own anti-particle through the same interaction process. As a result, dark matter represents nearly all the luminous light in the universe. In this context, model predictions for the X boson decay into $\mu^+\mu^-$ and DM pair production in $e^+e^-$ collisions are provided.

In light of the minimal length concept, the Dyson equation for triaxial nuclei is re-examined, with the inherent symmetry breaking in space due to the minimal length being accounted for. Contrasting the usual Dyson equation solution that yields a prolate-gyrating low-energy state, the new solution, grounded in the generalized uncertainty principle, supports an oblate-gyrating ground state. This leads to the proposal of a novel collective motion operator for triaxial nuclei, with corresponding modified transition strengths. Notably, the new strengths exhibit decreased values compared to the standard Dyson equation results, with significant changes observed in transition strengths between states of the same spin but different parity. This research paves the way for exploring the minimal length impact on nuclear collective dynamics through future studies incorporating the GUP effect within the framework of the Brownian collective model.

The properties of a type of complementary array, known as a Golay complementary set, are utilized to create synthesized arrays with specific four-dimensional properties. By utilizing a particular type of Golay code, known as a dual Golay code, a subset of such arrays is classified as pseudo-orthogonal. A classification of the remaining arrays is provided and they are referred to as non-pseudo-orthogonal GCSAs. This reference serves to document the characteristics of these arrays, including their propagation characteristics, and to record the various methods of constructing new GCSAs from existing ones.

Change detection in high-dimensional spectral data sets poses a challenge due to hyperspectral imaging's large data sets and the intricacies of alteration detection, making it a difficult task for machine learning models. Deep convolutional autoencoders, particularly those trained on encoded spectral features, exhibit potential in detecting alterations without requiring ground truth data. Nevertheless, the methods' effectiveness rely heavily on the features learned and the distance metric employed for comparing feature representations. This paper examines whether combining encoders that train on different features, including spatial and spectral properties, can enhance alteration detection. Our proposed approach involves using a feature combination model that merges the encoded representations from two separate autoencoders to improve detection performance. Experiments on the HIPAI Salinas dataset show that the proposed method performs better compared to previous methods.

By utilizing molecular dynamics simulations of ethane and octane in different temperatures, spanning from -200 to 350 K, our study investigates the residual entropy due to the coexistence of liquid and vapor phases. The simulated data is matched with an extension of the theory developed by Lopez and Kissinger to calculate the excess entropy of pure substances. In relation to the properties of real fluids, our results indicate a connection between residual entropy and viscosity at a molecular level, also observed in real fluids. The models used for simulating the pure substances influence the outcome, a topic that has been extensively explored in previous research. The found correlation between residual entropy and viscosity could contribute to the development of statistical models that describe complex liquid-vapor transitions by means of the connective partition function theory.

A cosmological model is proposed that integrates the cycle of the universe and simulates a complex picture of the universe's expansion. In this theory, dark energy acts as a bridge linking the expansion phases, achieving a stable state through a balance that mimics the effects of dark matter. Consequently, the predicted behaviors of dark matter and dark energy within this model align with the observational standards of the $\Lambda$CDM model. As such, the proposed cosmological model boasts predictive consistency with current astronomical data and also allows for predictive insights into future research findings. Additionally, the accuracy of the predicted observables is assessed using simulation data.

The Invariant-set hypothesis, a superdeterministic theory potentially reconciling local realism with quantum mechanics, is explored within a hidden-variable framework.  Utilizing a modified version of Bell's theorem, an examination is conducted to assess this model's ability to satisfy the requirements of local realism.  Consequently, this paper derives strong, local realism constraints on the properties of any underlying hidden variables, and it becomes evident that meeting these constraints poses a substantial challenge for the Invariant-set model, suggesting that it fails to address the apparent paradox between local realism and quantum mechanics.  As such, this theory does not appear capable of resolving the long-standing mystery of quantum nonlocality.

This study investigates whether Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can be effectively executed on constrained IoT devices, such as Single Board Computers and IoT modules like NVIDIA Jetson Nano and Intel Movidius FPGD, in order to streamline the process of identifying key phrases from text data, enabling more data analysis tasks to be performed on the device itself. Initially, the project determines the optimal input size for text data that can be processed by these devices while also evaluating various CNN architectures in terms of their accuracy and performance. Notably, it was found that NVIDIA's Jetson TX2 board outperformed other devices in processing power. Furthermore, the study identifies that CNNs can achieve comparable accuracy, up to 96.67%, when processing single sentences, while also considering the impact of word limitation on text data quality. Finally, the project explores additional optimizations such as data augmentation and merging multiple CNN models to enhance the devices' overall accuracy and performance.

We examine the relationship between two statistical models, one for walk patterns and the other for dimer arrangements, and demonstrate that their equivalent versions can be formulated as a path integral framework within a two-dimensional space. By attaching a gauge field to this framework, we are able to use known solutions for the dimer model to derive an exact expression for the Schrödinger fermion's wave function in a zero-mode approximation, particularly when the gauge field is set to zero. Furthermore, by incorporating the gauge field's influence, we find an analytical solution for the path integral and a semi-analytical expression for the wave function of the complex Weyl fermion in a $U(N)\times U(N)$ gauge field with constant expectation values. Interestingly, we also outline a method to derive the fermion's one-loop effective action. By removing the fermionic nature from the path integral, we can observe the emergence of a $T=T_{c}$ phase transition in the dimer arrangement model, along with a comparison with the exact outcome from the triconnected dimer model on a flat surface. Also, we connect this approach with another method to derive the effective action via a gauge-invariant integral over bosonic components stemming from a $U(N)\times U(N)$ gauge field. Lastly, we explore additional applications of this approach in integrating the gauge field's influence in the context of quasi-exactly solvable models and the calculation of symmetry-respected effective potential forms.

This research introduces a novel extension to the Group-Lasso, aiming to tackle a key challenge in a high-dimensional, nominal feature space. The proposed method chooses one variable from each group, one at a time, using an enhanced Group-Lasso framework. The standard Group-Lasso framework is expanded upon by making two key assumptions. Firstly, each group's features exhibit a linear relationship with the group's target variable, and secondly, all groups are uniquely determined. These conditions allow for the development of a multi-stage algorithm that incorporates an improved version of the standard Group-Lasso estimator. Assuming the data meet these criteria, it is demonstrated that the new method yields an accurate solution, and through simulation experiments and real-world applications, its performance surpasses that of competing techniques.

In recent years, the development of embedded real-time systems has increased rapidly, with the introduction of Linux and various hypervisors. Using a hypervisor to manage embedded real-time systems is a cost-effective solution that ensures long-term system development and expansion. Embedding a hypervisor on embedded operating systems is a straightforward approach that leverages the multiplexing capabilities of hardware virtualization technology, thereby preventing Linux from being embedded directly on the hardware. Nevertheless, this method introduces overhead, necessitating the minimization of overhead costs to facilitate the efficient execution of real-time systems. With the T-Visor hypervisor designed for x86 hardware, our research focuses on striking a balance between the interoperability of guest Linux systems and hypervisor overhead efficiency. Our analytical model calculates the upper limits of VLT and EMT values, with the results validated through experimental testing, demonstrating T-Visor's competitive performance relative to existing solutions.

When working with panoramic images, distortions such as radial distortion, geometrical transformations, and anisotropic scaling need to be addressed through the use of mapping functions, which are identified as "minimal answers" in this context. The key constraint for these mapping functions is maintaining a stitch-free field in the transform domain, making the identification of the optimal minimal answer a complex task. This study introduces a novel gradient prior derived from the camera's movement, often referred to as "gravitational force," and utilizes it to minimize the distortions in the image. The proposed approach relies on the use of a gravitational free-form objective field, thus avoiding the need for local optimization techniques. The results show that utilizing this gravitational prior results in an significant reduction in image distortions, and that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods on a dataset composed of 20 outdoor, large-scale panoramic images.

Our research explores the effect of variable parameter heterogeneity in large networks, focusing on its impact on the dynamics of chimeras - systems displaying dual coherent and incoherent behavior. By examining networks where all nodes receive input from a common source, we investigated the role of heterogeneity in the transfer parameters in maintaining chimeras. Findings indicate that in random heterogeneity scenarios, incoherent activity is reduced with increased disorder, yet remains present at sufficiently large scales; in contrast, the emergence of chimeras is more readily associated with the initial order of networks, which can be further manipulated by introducing external influences.

Contemporary controller learning methods prioritize optimizing performance in stable environments, but their reliability is severely compromised when faced with uncertainties in practical scenarios. To address this, we develop a novel framework that synergizes adversarial training and probabilistic model-driven optimization. This approach not only enhances network robustness but also promotes controller reliability through a sequential guidance process. By translating perturbations into informative signals, we demonstrate that our model can accurately predict controllability and efficiently detect disturbances. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our solution in achieving superior reliability and robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Building upon multi-layered diagrams introduced in \cite{diagram paper}, we have derived a generalisation of Taylor's slice construction for $E_\infty$-algebras from a multi-layered diagram. This construction is related to a graded version of the Taylor slice ring known as the higher slice ring. By applying the concept of homomorphism rings, we have further developed the underlying theory of higher slice rings from a universal algebra perspective. As a result, the higher slice ring can be achieved through the incorporation of a subring. Moreover, the concept of reductive slices in the context of the Medvedovski-Willner ring of binary formal polynomials demonstrates the applicability of the higher slice ring in the study of rigid polynomials. In conclusion, the higher slice ring presents a means to create a substructure comprising rigid polynomials within the Medvedovski-Willner ring.

Quantum error metrics such as the multiparty entanglement entropy are vital in assessing both classical correlations within localized patterns and quantum entanglement throughout the system. In this study, we examine the properties of multiparty mutual information in a one-dimensional chaotic complex network with random tensor elements. We identify correlation patterns within nearest-neighbor and higher-order arrangements of these tensors by decomposing the network and analyzing its fractal structure, which exhibits similar behaviors regardless of the network size. By using this insight, we develop a method to estimate the entire network's mutual information entropy from the correlation properties of the tensor matrix's principal eigenvalue. This self-similar fractal pattern allows for the generalization of our findings to arbitrarily large systems, making the proposed estimation method scalable. Moreover, we found that reducing the network's size by half results in a significant decrease in entropy by an amount proportional to the entropy of the reduced system, which establishes a relationship analogous to the fractal entropy loss principle. By applying this principle to larger systems, we can derive an estimation formula for the entropy of a large system based on the entropy of smaller, related systems.

Living organisms inherit characteristics from their ancestors, leading to a wide
array of morphologies and behaviors that are passed down heritably. In contrast,
stochastic processes in physics and biology that rely on thermal fluctuations do
not incorporate this heritable information. This review explores the links
between heritable information and Markov processes, demonstrating their use in
modeling complex stochastic systems in physics and biology. It also highlights
issues with methods that neglect this heritable information due to their
suppositional nature, as well as the supplementary information required to
fully comprehend their dynamics. The discussion, therefore, seeks to integrate
these perspectives within the context of statistical mechanics.

The generalized Hénon map, a three-dimensional iteration of the form $x_{n+1}=x_n+\alpha y_n-\beta x_n^3$, plays a significant role in understanding three-dimensional dynamics and has some connections to the Hénon map, the Lorenz system, and other prominent systems in the field. Despite its importance, this iteration receives relatively little attention in the literature. However, recent research indicates that this map can form chaotic attractors, which are visually similar to those of the Lorenz system. Our goal in this article is to showcase the chaotic nature of these three-dimensional generalized Hénon maps by exhibiting the chaotic attractors that they can form. To accomplish this goal, we examine the key parameters required to form these chaotic attractors, which are determined by the values of $\alpha$ and $-\beta$. Our method for determining these parameters is based on a condition for attracting behavior in a pullback version of the generalized Hénon map. This condition, which is derived using the Birkhoff Oscillation Theorem, can be applied to any pullback system of the form $x'(t) = f(x(t))$, where $f$ is a nonlinear function. Our analysis indicates that the pullback system must have a unique attracting invariant set $\mathcal{A}$ within a bounded region, which may not necessarily correspond to a pullback attractor in the sense of the pullback semiflow. Based on this method, our research identifies

The essence of general relativity's non-linear nature resides in the concept of gravitational holonomy, a pivotal tool for exploring the curvature of space-time. Variants of the holonomy formula have been proposed in the literature, leading to multiple representations. This paper undertakes a comprehensive examination, showing that distinct formulations merely represent different aspects of a single, fundamental form. Moreover, the study delves into the underlying structure, identifying both commonalities and divergences across different formulations, and predicting that the influence of gravitational holonomy will stimulate innovative research in the field.

In the context of affine Lie algebras, we analyze the distributions associated with highest weight modules of specific type A lattices, focusing on standard and twisted modules. We derive explicit formulas for these distributions in terms of modules multiplicable by two or three, and verify that they align with pre-existing results for NSCFT conformal blocks. Building on this, we outline a approach to simplify distributions associated with all levels, leveraging the concept of 'double and triple basements'.

Investigating the tunneling process of a particle through a potential barrier,
our research reveals that slight distortions in the particle's internal spin structure
are contingent on this process's specific details and timing. Furthermore, these
spin fluctuations can be utilized to calculate the particle's relative velocity
as it approaches the barrier. By considering a particle with an internal spin of
1/2, our analysis based on the Pauli theory demonstrates that slight distortions
in its spin direction indicate a particle approaching a barrier from the front,
whereas a fluctuation in the opposite direction indicates the particle is
approaching from the rear. By applying our theoretical model to an atom, our
research shows that atomically induced spin disturbances can modulate a spin
clock's reading, leading to a shift of up to 1.4 hours over a 50-year period.
Conversely, our theoretical model is contrasted with experimental findings from
Bormann et al. in a specific study on particle tunneling, revealing an apparent
discrepancy between our predicted spin fluctuations and their observed spin
modulations through Larmor interference.

Recent research suggests that nucleons are composed of various distinct phases of quark distribution, such as "salad" and "rice bowl" configurations. Our findings indicate that, in non-relativistic mesons with a P-wave, certain dominant quark arrangements within these nuclerons take the form of a circular "ring" surrounding a central quark, with all other configurations being less prevalent. Consequently, a prominent quark distribution known as the "dominant twist distribution profile" emerges. Our research identifies the dominant twist distribution profiles for P-wave mesons, including the light vector mesons and their radial counterparts, for both light and heavy quark contents. We then utilize this information to compute the quark distribution functions and their moments for the studied mesons. Our results match prior research on these distribution functions.

We're examining a model of two-component Bose-Einstein condensates with a difference in their chemical potential, undergoing a Metamorphosis like transformation with a periodic change in this potential difference. This model can be compared to that of two-state systems switching between different values under external influence. Unlike linear responses, the switch mechanism here involves a gradual change, resulting in a complex phenomenon where superfluid behavior is lost and an effective Bogoliubov approximation is unable to predict the transition to non-superfluidity. Yet, in a specific case where the switch is like a step function and changes at a particular point, the transition can be accurately predicted using a combination of linear responses from different directions. This model can be experimentally achieved by using overlapping lasers in a laboratory setting.

This review expands on our previous work that derived the BMS algebra from soft theoreies in gauge theories, specifically considering classical solutions and conservative charges. We provide detailed mathematical derivations to support the main outcomes. Additionally, the paper explores new applications of the BMS algebra, examining conservation laws at the quantum level within quantum electrodynamics and highlighting a quantum paradox tied to Kullback-Leibler charges. A thorough analysis of this paradox is presented along with the paradoxon's resoluion.

This study introduces the Neural Structure for Online Ensemble Continued
Learning (NOEL), a novel adaptation of ensemble methods capable of continuous
learning. Traditional online ensemble methods struggle with adaptive learning,
typically requiring a frame-based adaptation approach. However, such approaches
preclude collaborative learning among ensemble members, as well as online
adaptation to see each other's performance. To address this, NOEL enables
adaptive learning with an online hierarchical mechanism, allowing individual
sub-ensemble adaptation and ensemble-level adaptation across training epochs.
Furthermore, NOEL enables in-epoch adaptation, allowing sub-ensembles to learn
from one another. Notably, NOEL performs competitively with state-of-the-art
methods on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, offering improved scalability through reduced
computational and memory requirements.

In this study, we establish novel connections between Euler-Lagrange equations and their harmonics within a four-dimensional framework. A specific class of metrics has been identified as particularly suitable for analysis. Four-dimensional conformally equivalent superharmonic functions can be linked to cohomology classes within a 3D Euclidean space, enabling the construction of specific classes of metrics and their corresponding Laplace equations.

In this study, we derive specific formulas for the number of permutation groups with bases in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and examine the properties of permutation functions and complete permutation functions with respect to subfields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$. We then proceed to compute the counts of permutation functions and complete permutation functions that satisfy a particular degree condition over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and provide explicit formulae for the sums of permutation function degrees and complete permutation function degrees, respectively.

A major public health concern in many low-income countries, chronic intestinal
infection by parasitic worms causes severe discomfort, hinders children's ability
to learn, and impedes economic development. To tackle this issue, accurate
diagnosis is essential but often eludes healthcare workers in these countries due
to the worms' tiny size, the alike appearance of different species, and the
presence of non-infectious worms in the same area, all posing a challenge for
manual identification. To address this problem, a novel deep learning method
utilizing Bayesian segmentation is presented to categorize parasitic worms in
images taken from standard microscopes. To evaluate the effectiveness of
this approach, a comprehensive dataset of CDC-D worms and T. blagovichevi from
various locations has been established, including 1015 images of CDC-D worms and
520 images of T. blagovichevi. Results show that the proposed method can achieve
highly effective classification and segmentation of worms, laying the groundwork
for future diagnostic tools. Furthermore, the potential of this technique is
also explored for diagnosing a range of intestinal parasites using a single
image.

This work introduces a new method for estimating a family of non-zero-sum investment
and reinsurance strategies using finite-time conditional least-squares for two-dimension Markov
processes that model regime-switching. We provide explicit formulas for the optimal model parameters
in each state, then extend the estimation technique to a broad scenario involving arithmetic, geometric,
or logarithmic reinsurance strategies in combination with various asset models, such as Black-Scholes,
Black-Scholes with jumps, the stochastic volatility model, and the Bergom-Brennan model with jumps.

This paper introduces a novel control technique that leverages a stochastic dual simplex algorithm to create a control law, combined with a genetic filter to refine the design. The proposed method enables the design of proportional-integral-derivative (PID) and proportional-nodal-derivative (PND) controllers via linear parameter-varying (LPV) model representation. The proposed controller design is demonstrated on a highly nonlinear nonlinear generic jet aircraft model, achieving stable flight despite challenging conditions including flight modes such as steady state, takeoff, landing, and gust. The research illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in designing control laws for highly complex aircraft models, encompassing all three dimensions of the flight envelope.

This article examines the significance of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions in effective field theories. It highlights that several prominent pion-nucleon scattering observables, such as elastic differential cross-sections and polarization, are inherently linked to the inherent characteristics of nucleons. This connection is rooted in the principle of unitarity and manifests through the presence of resonances and infrared divergences, which can be adequately represented using effective field theory techniques that respect the underlying symmetry of the strong nuclear forces. The study provides arguments suggesting that high-energy experiments won't reveal information about the degree of irreducible (or non-derivable) low-energy constants, as exemplified by analyses of various experimentally measurable quantities such as the pion-nucleon decay length, the width of the Δ resonance, and the non-derivable constant influencing elastic scattering polarization. These constants are (or will be) directly measurable via current or proposed experiments involving the study of the phase shifts, electromagnetic form factors and Pion-Nucleon Scattering Cross Section.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment employs a sophisticated pixel module with low-interference readout systems, including novel analog signals that bypass conventional digital recording methods. An innovative reconstruction method, known as pilot running, was utilized to capture these analog signals from select modules. The resulting data, stored offline, were analyzed to extract pixel hit information. This study focuses on the quantitative assessment of pilot-recorded signals, their contribution to total hit information, and the consistency of pilot data across various modules. Additionally, we compare pixel hit resolution from conventional digitized data with those derived from pilot-recorded analog signals.

We analyzed the X-ray luminosity versus redshift for 1,117 active galactic nuclei selected from the Hyper Suprime-Cam wide survey, focusing on a single band with $10^{43}$ to $10^{47}$ erg s$^{-1}$. Our study used machine learning to classify the host galaxies into two groups: single bright core or multiple faint cores. The machine learning algorithm was trained on prior studies using smaller samples and then applied to the new data, yielding a classification accuracy of nearly 90%. The effectiveness of this method led to a detailed analysis of the host galaxies' morphologies, which revealed that approximately 32% have multiple faint cores, while about 68% have single bright cores. The distribution of host galaxy properties did not correlate with their morphological features. Additionally, our research found that galaxies with multiple faint cores are more massive, have higher star formation rates, and are experiencing moreSupernova explosion energy releases than those with single bright cores. The findings from this study provide the groundwork for a future examination of the host galaxies' morphological development using the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey's extensive data.

In the context of infinite nuclear and neutron matter, through the study of average properties of bound neutron pairs, we explore the effects of high-frequency two-neutron emissions that satisfy certain conditions. Utilizing the Spectral Function approach, we employed the No Core Nucleosynthesis model to simulate weak interactions between neutrons and alpha particles within a copper nucleus, and extracted distributions of two-neutron energy using the coherent momentum distribution of the copper nucleus. Our calculations demonstrate that, for a given energy range, the average properties of bound neutron pairs exhibit negligible variations which could indicate a possible stabilization of such systems against high-energy excitations. While the present study does not provide conclusive evidence of neutron clustering, it lays the groundwork for future investigations focusing on the phase-space distributions of correlated neutron pairs, potentially leading to the creation of neutron-depleted clusters.

We are studying complex-valued deep networks with co-domain equality, meaning their outputs must match in both magnitude and phase. These networks are particularly relevant for applications like beamforming, channel state information, and image and video processing. Initially, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a function to realize a complex-valued deep network with co-domain equality. Furthermore, we developed specific techniques for constructing complex-valued deep networks using real-valued layers, which we then applied to various classification and regression problems. Our results also reveal new insights into the capabilities of real-valued deep networks.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  This saturation momentum serves as a scaling parameter applying to various processes in high-energy collisions involving small systems.  In such systems, the momentum transfer squared becomes directly proportional to the power of the saturation momentum, indicating a form of geometrical scaling.  This study first establishes that geometrical scaling exists in a particular scale of the momentum transfer.  Subsequently, it demonstrates that geometrical scaling also exists in the x-dependence of the structure functions for various scales.  Furthermore, the study makes predictions regarding the existence of geometrical scaling in various other high-energy collisions and suggests a means of determining the saturation momentum using relativistic heavy-ion collision experiments.  Specifically, it shows that the transverse energy per unit rapidity per unit transverse area generated when protons collide with other protons at high energies varies inversely according to a power of the collision energy.  This variation is similar to that observed for the average transverse momentum as a function of the center-of-mass energy in central heavy-ion collisions.

Our understanding of the initial conditions of the Milky Way's outer regions, as evidenced by its oldest low-metal and hyper-metal stars, is crucial for deciphering the galaxy's early history but remains unclear. To explore how different elements were formed and evolved, we studied the chemical compositions of several groups of ancient low-metal and high-metal stars within the outer reaches of the Milky Way, focusing on the ratios of two key chemical elements. The results reveal significant variations in the chemical compositions of different low-metal stars as well as a relationship between metal content and chemical compositions across various groups of stars. In contrast, we found no indication of varying initial chemical compositions among the high-metallicity stars. The data support the theory that these low-metal stars originated from a nearby dwarf galaxy that underwent significant chemical disruptions during merging, whereas the high-metallicity stars likely originated from the galaxy's central region. The chemical compositions of the low-metal stars suggest two distinct chemical patterns, indicating different chemical manufacturing processes and offering potential insights into the galaxy's early conditions. Furthermore, we estimate that chemical-enrichment gradients within the dwarf galaxy were relatively low, similar to what is observed in modern dwarf galaxies. The study provides a framework for deciphering chemical history signs by analyzing the chemical compositions of outer Milky Way stars.

When evaluating complex machine learning forecasts, traditional accuracy metrics are inadequate, as they overlook the significant impact of easy-to-predict opportunities on a model's performance. For instance, in the context of predicting financial literacy levels, a model that consistently forecasts "not literate" for all individuals would achieve minimal accuracy when focusing on the main classification outcomes, but would incorrectly attribute this performance to the model's complexity. In this work, we develop a novel performance assessment framework that accounts for biased classification, consistent classification, and easy-to-predict probabilities, providing corresponding statistical tests. We also create an empirical analysis tool that utilizes these concepts and illustrates its applications with a unique dataset collecting forecasts on financial literacy from neural networks. We investigate how different network architectures impact performance and introduce a new dataset with labels for hidden layer activations, after a series of experiments, finding that more complex models do not necessarily lead to better financial literacy forecasting.

We've created a neural network from a specific type of quantum computer model called the Squid, which we've found achieves remarkable results on complex image classification tasks. Additionally, our research demonstrates that a Squid-based model not only surpasses conventional machine learning models but also reaches a key milestone in the transition from classical to quantum computing, all while using much less energy. We believe that using the Squid model as a foundation for deep learning can offer a new pathway for applying quantum computing in machine learning, even if it's largely classical in nature. We've made our code available to the public, which includes a new method for training large-scale artificial neural networks by leveraging GPU and TPU parallel processing.

Researchers, Chen and Zhang, have examined distorted product manifolds. 
Key takeaways from their study include: 
  a) Sufficient conditions for such manifolds to be warped products have been established. 
  b) Those conditions are also shown to be necessary for certain types of warped products. 
  c) Researcher Deng and Chen previously found that a specific warped product satisfying a particular condition could not be a segmental product, and this negative result is now generalised to distorted products.

We propose utilizing diamond-based color center technology to explore inactive isotopes in the low-energy range of nuclear recoil spectroscopy. The current research account is divided into two sections. The initial section provides an overview of recent advancements in paleoecologic research, concentrating on the general principles of measurements, data analysis techniques, and relevant results. The second section delves into the specifics of employing diamond-based color center technology for this type of investigation, examining its potential advantages and discussing the initial study conducted to verify the sensitivity of this approach.

Colloidal particles experience varying speeds in different chemical reactions within a fluid. Our study explores how multiple particles move within a complex environment where the chemical reaction rate changes. The particles' behavior is influenced by both the fluid's reaction rate and the repulsive forces between the particles. To achieve efficient fluid mixing, the particles typically converge toward regions of the fluid with the lowest chemical reaction rates. However, if the repulsive forces between the particles are significant, they may avoid such convergence and instead move toward regions where their movement is least restricted, which often corresponds to the region with an intermediate reaction rate. By analyzing how external forces affect the particles, we demonstrate that strong repulsive forces can actually lead to the particles converging with the fluid flow and clearing the fluid of particles through enhanced mixing. On the other hand, we find that external forces can prevent this mixing, leaving the fluid with a mixture of different particle sizes. The remaining mixture is characterized by particle-rich regions surrounded by rings of lower particle concentration, forming a pattern known as negative-negative negative domains. The position of the domains depends on both the size of the external forces and the size of the particles. The results of our study are supported by a non-traditional method of data analysis, as well as a companion study that uses advanced numerical tools to simulate the behavior of the fluid and particles under different conditions. The study predicts that as long as the external forces continue to act on the fluid, the fluid will remain mixed, but when the external

This study delves into the theoretical framework underlying seniority physics within weakly-coupled lattice models featuring complex spin-orbit interactions. These systems exhibit considerable ground-state spin-separation characteristics when employing seniority-based constraints to identify their ordered magnetic phases. A distinct type of spectral topological feature known as the "magnetoron" is explored, where the interplay between seniority constraints and spin properties yields a intricate distribution of gapped phases, each linked to unique magneton configurations. A comprehensive examination of phase regulations reveals how the interplay between spin and valley sectors leads to intricate distributions of gapped and non-gapped states, where magnetrons represent key indicators for identifying states with zero edges and internal magnetic ordering, further highlighting the regulatory effect of seniority constraints on phase transitions between topological and non-topological states.

Many contagious diseases spread rapidly across specific populations, often tracking the progression of a single "seed" virus within a confined area. Research indicates that the outbreak pattern of such infections often follows a standard geometric pattern. Consequently, a straightforward clustering approach has been developed to identify potential epicenters of outbreaks. This method consistently produces more accurate results compared to alternative, complex statistical techniques. Furthermore, a numerical example demonstrates that the new approach is effective in predicting the initial spread of an infection and yields a significantly longer outbreak period when compared with established models.

This paper introduces a novel method for processing two-dimensional angular data, such as CMB maps, that expands upon the maximum likelihood estimator by incorporating external prior information in a Gaussian framework. The proposed approach addresses the inherent circular asymmetry present in angular data around the point origin, yielding more effective results for both individual features and overall datasets, while also providing an option to utilize non-uniform priors. Two case studies are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of our method, showcasing its applications in both the presence of a single anomalous feature and a realistic CMB dataset simulation. Furthermore, the method is made available in a Python package called liest, which offers a versatile tool for statistical analysis.

Our research focuses on a reinforcement learning setup called goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, where an agent learns to achieve a range of goals by receiving rewards and feedback that outline each objective. However, the field's progress has been hindered by the method's poor performance in more complex, multi-agent environments that hearken back to classic multi-agent games and involve communication. Previous attempts at developing this kind of reinforcement learning setup have largely been met with limited success due to the particular low-entropy methods employed, as well as the lack of a meaningful benchmark to gauge their performance. We present a novel method that overcomes these issues by leveraging the use of distributional rewards and a novel language generation technique based on a goal-oversseeing transformer model. Our method achieves this goal without requiring the ability to directly communicate. We develop a suite of highly customizable, high-entropy multi-player games that serve as challenging testing grounds for this kind of reinforcement learning setup, and we show through our experiments that it leads to the achievement of all desired objectives, as demonstrated by both the completion rates and the smoothness of the learned plans obtained by our method.

Quantum channel tomography is crucial for understanding quantum processes, but existing methods have significant drawbacks. This research introduces shadow quantum channel tomography, an innovative approach that involves viewing a quantum channel as a combination of two classical channels. One of these classical channels represents the classical shadow of a quantum state, while the other accounts for the residual information that's not accessible through this classical view. We present algorithms for determining these channels, which enables us to calculate key metrics like the trace distance and Fisher information for quantum states, without needing explicit access to them. Notably, the largest error in calculating the trace distance stems from both channels' inaccuracies and can be tightly bounded by the trace distances of the quantum channels. Furthermore, the shadow tomography of a quantum channel is equivalent to the scenario where we're given random measurements, which correlates with the number of qubits in the quantum system. We demonstrate that the shadow of an N-qubit quantum state can be identified with a time complexity of $\mathrm{O}(N^{\frac{7}{6}} \cdot \log N)$ using a single qubyte quantum computer, which is comparable to the $\mathrm{O}(N^{\log_2 N})$ time required to perform a quantum Fourier transform. This research marks the first attempt to develop accurate estimators for fundamental metrics like the trace distance and Fisher information for quantum states using near-term Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.

This research provides a comprehensive set of inequalities for shapes with a positive Cheeger constant within a two-dimensional plane. These inequalities pertain to various functions, including the perimeter, area, and a Cheeger constant itself. Additionally, we establish that any planar shape with a Cheeger constant close to 1 must have a distinctive, simply shaped boundary. This outcome restricts the possible values of a related constant for these shapes, as well as their boundary geometries. Finally, our analysis introduces a relevant problem involving the minimum Cheeger constant for ellipses, prompting a practical consideration: what is the Cheeger constant for a shape consisting of the difference between two n-sided polygons?

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, serving under the umbrella of "Flying Internet," seek to establish a connection even when ground fibers are inaccessible. Maintaining a continuous connection requires the deployment of multiple UAVs, each covering a specific area, with their collective shadowing patterns overlapping to ensure worldwide coverage. Optimization of UAV flight paths is examined, with each vehicle covering maximum area in a given time frame. An integer linear programming model and a heuristic-based solution, inspired by MapReduce, aim to determine the best deployment strategy, minimizing the number of required UAVs to achieve this. An optimized solution is found through the application of a local search algorithm. Results demonstrate that the proposed heuristic offers an efficient, near-optimal solution with a high degree of accuracy.

This study provides a detailed Rogerson chain analysis of the multiple body instability in bilayer graphene's Coulomb interactions. Starting with a model that incorporates thermal fluctuations in the system's effective theory, we employ a model-based renormalization group approach to analyze the system's dynamics and ultimately uncover the emergence of multiple body excitations due to Coulomb interactions. We further validate our findings by demonstrating that the system in question can be effectively reduced to a well-established Rogerson chain model, which was initially discovered in studies focused on the one-dimensional electron system's instability. We take a comprehensive approach in our rigorous derivation and obtain explicit expressions for all relevant coupling constants of the Rogerson chain model up to the fourth order in energy. Furthermore, we leverage these new constants to predict the presence of zero-mode excitations, one-dimensional plasmons, chiral states, edge solitons, polaritons, two-dimensional electron liquids, and charge density waves as potential states in Coulomb coupled bilayer graphene. Notably, our analysis also uncovers the existence of a new regime in Coulomb interactions in low energy domain which has not been previously reported. We further leverage our new findings to predict the quantitative relationship between Coulomb and Chern-Simons terms in the effective model, which in turn allows us to determine the existence of non-abelian excitations in Coulomb coupled bilayer graphene.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. Consequently, controlling conformations of molecular substances is a crucial research area. This study experimentally examines how the temperature influences the conformation of Tb bearing fullerene molecule, Sc2TbN@C80, supported on another molecule, Nb (Tb = 1-8). By employing high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy on sample, Sc2TbN@C80/Nb, conformational changes with respect to the temperature were observed. This involved analyzing the distribution of molecule's heights and using elastic force field simulation to determine the energy difference between two conformations, up-down and side-side. Ultimately, findings from this study reveal that as temperature increases from 10 K to 70 K, molecule, Sc2TbN@C80, exhibits multiple conformational changes from up-down to side-side configuration. Also, with further increase in the temperature to 100 K, the conformation up-up emerges and prevails at higher temperatures. Moreover, at temperature of 70 K, the energy up-down and side-side are in equal proportion. Interestingly, up-down and side-side conformations show strong self-assembling properties with respect to each other. Furthermore, at temperature of 60 K, the energy up-up and side-side are in equal proportion. However, up-down and up-up conformations show weak non-covalent interaction with respect to other.

The number of IoT devices is rapidly expanding, with a huge number of new devices being connected every day. Unfortunately, a large portion of these "smart" devices come equipped with insecure default passwords that can be easily accessed by hackers. Additionally, many manufacturers often overlook or neglect to update these security flaws even after being notified. Furthermore, low-energy IoT devices often struggle to efficiently utilize high computational resources like encryption, making them an attractive target for cyber threats. This study examines various lightweight algorithms, aiming to identify the most suitable solutions for securing IoT devices against potential threats. An evaluation of several lightweight cryptographic algorithms was conducted using the NIST lightweight cryptographic survey, with a focus on measuring their computational overhead for encryption and decryption processes. The aim was to determine which algorithms were suitable for application on low-energy devices such as IoT sensors.

A novel framework called Sequential Bayesian Trial Formulation (SBTF), originally designed for medical trials, has been expanded to include complex measurement types beyond simple binary readings. This process models uncertainty using a multidimensional probability density function (PDF) which is updated with each measurement, leveraging all previous data. We've established a general strategy for incorporating new measurement information, specifically using PDF conditioning for incorporating new data. In addition to this, we have developed a method for determining when to sample based on measures such as expected change or confidence intervals. This framework has been applied to a series of simulations mimicking a Ramsey-type experiment commonly used in nuclear physics and thermometry, employing Bayesian methods to improve measurement precision. Simulation results indicate that SBTF can facilitate more efficient measurements, enabling similar precision with fewer measurements compared to traditional approaches, particularly benefiting experiments with measurement uncertainties dominated by statistical variance.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and random walk theories, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is proposed, measured by the nodes' surplus of triangle inequality violations, which reflects the degree of geographical concentration of the network's triangle structures. This method is further developed into two linear-time variants, depending on whether the network's triangle structures are inclusive or exclusive of the shortest paths. The proposed multi-scale centrality has a theoretical connection to other network metrics, and its applicability is demonstrated through its analysis of both synthetic and real-world networks, as well as its comparison with other centrality methods in characterizing multi-scale leads to new insights into network topology.

The Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity is presented as a simplified model for gravitational fields, consistent with the principles of Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, yet formulated using a simplified approach. A derivative of Newton's theory, this new approach yields the same results for weak gravitational fields, yet offers a more streamlined and intuitive framework for understanding gravitational phenomena. A previous paper developed the mathematical underpinnings of this theory, while this paper explores its practical applications, starting with an examination of the planet Mars. By assuming the planet Mars is spherical and possessing a uniform mass distribution, various physical parameters can be calculated, revealing key characteristics such as its rotation period, equatorial bulging, and gravitational field properties. A comparative analysis with data from the NASA Mars Atlas, compiled on September 29, 1965, demonstrates that the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity accurately predicts many of Mars' physical attributes, while also providing insight into the prospects for observing gravitational phenomena on Mars.

We are concentrating on the different types of matrix pencil families, such as canonical, characteristic, and Fless matrices, which all originate from a given matrix. To date, a comprehensive and structured description of these families has yet to be achieved. This work aims to establish connections between various established and proposed classifications of matrix pencils, as well as to clarify the relationships between them, through the concept of rigidity. Additionally, we are defining a new concept called extended D-matrices and establishing its connections to the rigorous equivalence classes of matrix pencils. These findings are also extended to the world of blocks.

A geometric method is developed to identify T-dual torus bundles with a specific type of twist. The employed notation provides a local construction of these bundles, which are denoted as $\mathcal{T}^n \times S^1$ with linear twist. The T-duality construction is performed by matching the leaf surfaces of the twisted torus bundles. It is demonstrated that the geometric approach yields the same results as the symplectic approach previously employed by the author.

We demonstrate that any dimension-d metric space whose embeddability in an n-vertex tree with radius r is straightforwardly embeddable to a 3r^2-dimension tree, and also find that this bound is optimal up to a logarithmic factor for a fixed d. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm that converts a planar metric with weight distribution (w_1,..., w_n) to a 4.5n^2-dimension planar metric, and also find that this mapping can be efficiently computed using a simple iterative method that selects adjacent vertices in the metric. However, we show that the problem of finding an embedding of a weighted complete graph in a 1-epsilon-dimension planar metric is essentially as difficult as solving the classical Minimum Bounded-Depth Spanning Trees problem.

We analyze global behavior in a class of map-based discrete-time dynamical systems that exhibit smooth, strongly monotonic properties across their domains of definition. Our analysis leverages new theoretical findings, and we demonstrate how these results can be applied to global bifurcation analysis in such systems.

The potential of noise-tolerant variational quantum algorithms lies in their ability to leverage arbitrary quantum systems without being affected by their state. We build upon this idea by integrating a procedure to eliminate errors caused by incorrect qubit conditions into the adaptive variational quantum eigensolver. Our modified version, QABVE, surpasses traditional VE in both efficiency and reliability, utilizing only a fraction of the classical steps while remaining resilient to both unitary drift and noisy qubits. Moreover, based on post-selection, QABVE achieves an average expectation value accuracy of 99.99% for the 2D Heisenberg model and 99.99% for the 2D transverse Ising model, as well as a average expectation value accuracy of 99.94% for the 2D ferromagnetic Heisenberg model, thus outperforming VE. Furthermore, QABVE's convergence is compared to that of the closed-loop variational quantum eigensolver, resulting in higher accuracy with fewer iterations, 99.99% for the 2D Heisenberg model and 99.99% for the 2D transverse Ising model, while the ferromagnetic Heisenberg model achieves an accuracy of 99.94%, thus demonstrating its superiority.

Our research presents a novel approach to generative learning, featuring a novel representation of data. The traditional method of generating sequences, based on a cause-to-effect assumption, starts with a representation of "causes" and uses it to generate "effects", is shown to be equivalent to a Bayesian approach where the posterior probability of "causes" given "effects" is maximized, by maximizing the probability of generating those "causes" and "effects" together. By utilizing maximum a posteriori estimates of "causes", this method is refined, making it the "profound" generative decoder. The application of this method to a simple task demonstrates better performance than other standard methods, including maximum likelihood learning and contrastive learning. Furthermore, its effectiveness in developing both intrinsic and extrinsic value in a multi-agent learning environment compares favorably with other standard methods.

The accuracy cosmology approach, incorporating the cosmic microwave background, large-scale structures, and baryon acoustic oscillations, enables a precise determination of cosmological parameters on Earth. This highly accurate method may resolve the long-standing conflict related to the "Hubble tension" between different cosmological observations. A key consideration in implementing accuracy cosmology is the potential contamination from an inflated gravitational wave background, potentially detectable by future laser interferometers like LIGO-Virgo, which could lead to a shift in the value of the dark energy's degeneracy parameter when detected. This study presents a detailed analysis of the accuracy cosmology technique, incorporating the impact of detectable gravitational waves from inflation and their effect on the value of the degeneracy parameter when detected by different instruments, including LIGO-Virgo and NANOGrav.

Two comets, C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) and C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS), were chosen for study within the COMET project, aiming to explore the capabilities of the ALMA Atacama Compact Array. Initially, researchers analyzed a 1-hour observation of ER61 on March 17, 2018, and obtained a 1.5"x1.5" image at 1.35 THz, providing H2O freeze-out mapping and H2O ice fractions. These fractions were compared to other comets, suggesting ER61's water content is lower. Also, varying levels of H2O and CS were found in the north and south sides of the comet, with increased thermal desorption on the sunlit side. It was further observed that CS levels on the unlit side could be equaled if the comet's water content was substantial, implying a water source beyond frost coverage, according to modelling. Secondly, a 2.4 hour observation of R2 on March 9, 2018, yielded a 3.5"x3.5" image at 1.75 THz, and with the addition of a large main-dish, it was found the emission was primarily from H2O. We examine the problem of producing a comprehensive speech dataset without
supervision, focusing on the part where we create spoken words from given audio
inputs. Our research shows that using a very basic two-layer network with
next-to-simplest continuous representations, we can achieve a high level of
speaking accuracy and also minimize the amount of computing power needed.
Compared to other, more complex systems that we tested, we can often produce
better results with significantly fewer resources. A generated speech dataset
created using this approach performed well in our experiments, and we provide
further insight into the dataset's construction and the simplicity of the
underlying system by showing examples of its spoken words.

In the context of complex quintessence, researchers have explored the effects of events in the universe's early stages on dark energy, focusing on the interaction between matter and dark energy.  They used the Tsallis entropy approach to develop an alternative to the original vitality, establishing an equation of state for dark energy and analyzing the radio of pressure and energy density without success.  Therefore, they decided to investigate the behavior of dark energy through the equation of state in the quintessence's Ludlows model.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems, pervasive in science and engineering, have traditionally been difficult to solve algorithmically. This research introduces a multi-objective optimization tool, incorporating the advanced multi-objective optimization algorithm, NSAII, which enhances computational efficiency through parallel processing. To enhance solution quality, the proposed tool integrates a state-of-the-art local search algorithm, which refines NSAII-generated candidate solutions. Additionally, the paper explores an improved Branch and Bound algorithm, combining its concept with NSAII to create BBNSAII. Performance evaluations of the proposed tools, utilizing real-world and established test cases, demonstrate their capability to tackle complex MO-MINLP problems efficiently, with an improved local search algorithm in NSAII yielding superior performance across multiple metrics.

The current work draws on the principles of Synthetic Differential Geometry, offering a new definition for specific groupoid categories: linked groupoids, integral linked groupoids, local integral linked groupoids, intrinsic groupoids, local groupoids, groupoid objects, and groupoids. We proceed to establish links between these categories and then demonstrate that each of these categories is equivalent to a subset of the local groupoid category. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between local groupoids and groupoids, showing that a local groupoid is equivalent to a groupoid if it exhibits not only a global section but also a coherent and dense morphism. Additionally, we show that the presence of a local section, a coherent and dense morphism, or a covering morphism on a groupoid object in a set allows us to prove the equivalence to a local integral linked groupoid, thus proving the statement of the thesis.

In the digital age, various data collections serve as digital heritage collections, offering up-to-date information and shedding light on past research, but they often operate in isolation due to lack of standardization and limited interoperability with other existing datasets. In this study, we highlight the importance of data interoperability, provide an overview of a gateway infrastructure that enables seamless data access, and present new cyberinfrastructure components to achieve this: data gateways and a multi-tenant federated data store. By supporting multi-tenant applications and innovative research approaches, these gateways empower researchers to analyze multiple datasets and foster novel insights, all while adhering to ethical research principles. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach using a biomedical example, specifically the combination of two large datasets related to COVID-19 research. By launching a multi-tenant COVID-19 data portal, we showcase the benefits of data exchange, safe data use, and data collaboration practices, ultimately facilitating more efficient research.

In numerous businesses, effective training of staff relies heavily on opinions expressed by customers, which can be positive, negative, or neutral in nature. Opinion-rich text data, coupled with specific topic focus, are referred to as reviews linked to aspects. Research in sentiment analysis capitalizes on trained models to break down reviews into targeted themes, ultimately expressing a sentiment for each. Current models, however, struggle to identify implicit sentiment expressed in a review, which can be likened to finding a needle in a haystack. To address this issue, we present a new approach, which combines supervised pre-training and contrastive learning to create a comprehensive sentiment-aware representation for the themes within reviews. Our proposed method is evaluated on various datasets and is found to perform superiorly compared to the latest state-of-the-art models across all the benchmarks.

Researchers interested in understanding how multiple variables connect through intermediaries often use a specific technique called mediation analysis. It allows researchers to assess whether variables have an impact by considering the role of intermediate factors. In studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state, researchers can make some assumptions that help establish causal links between variables, even in studies that don't provide a full range of data. This allows researchers to make some key assumptions about how variables work. In studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state, researchers can use data from these studies to find the average effects of variables, but there's a limitation to finding the direct effects of intermediate factors in studies that don't provide a full range of data.

In order to find the direct effects of intermediate factors in studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state, researchers must make some additional assumptions about how variables are connected. We will examine how researchers can make some specific assumptions in order to find the direct effects of intermediate factors in studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state. We will also discuss other potential assumptions that may be relevant in order to make conclusions in studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state.

In addition to making some specific assumptions about how variables are connected, researchers must also have information in order to make conclusions in studies that compare existing conditions with a desired state.
