This study aims to establish a distinctive polynomial, rooted in a specific graph theory concept, that can derive the transition probability matrix of an associated random walk. The investigation seeks to uncover key characteristics of this polynomial and demonstrate its primal role in analyzing Markov chains via the spectral theory of matrices and irreducible, strongly connected directed graphs.

In this work, we establish a fundamental theoretical framework for managing discrete-time events within a functional programming context based on Isabelle/HOL's higher-order logic. Discrete time is represented as a finite set of time points, including both absolute values and comparisons. A key aspect of this framework involves enriching functional data structures with time-related attributes, which facilitates the addition of temporal constraints and relationships. This approach enables the implementation of traditional recursive data structures on timed entities, featuring a range of useful theoretical principles, notably the ability to deduce fundamental properties of timeless data, the existence of unique temporal translations, and the capacity to break down multi-component functions into their individual time-based components.

This study aims to improve the accuracy of a coherent structure-based model for predicting wall-pressure fluctuations in turbulent flows near a wall. The model employs a simplified representation of the coherent structures in wall turbulence and has shown potential in modeling these flows. Nonetheless, it has yielded somewhat lower predictions of the fluctuating signal compared to measured data. To address this limitation, the model's performance is assessed using two distinct approaches. Firstly, an iterative data-mining technique is employed to refine the model's parameters and enhance predicted results. Secondly, the model is combined with a machine learning algorithm, which uses the model's outputs to predict the amplitude of wall-pressure fluctuations. These approaches facilitate a synergistic relationship between the model's physical assumptions and data analysis techniques. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated using two datasets, namely turbulent channel flow at moderate Reynolds numbers and turbulent channel flows with surface roughness. The resulting predictions accurately match the fluctuating signal and amplitude of wall-pressure fluctuations measured in the rough and smooth turbulent flows, respectively. The model's capabilities have also been validated using three additional datasets, including flows at varying Reynolds numbers, roughness heights, and channel configurations. Furthermore, the model's predictions have successfully replicated the stratification of wall-pressure fluctuations across various channels and scaling laws. Notably, the model's outputs have accurately aligned with the physical mechanisms governing wall-pressure fluctuations and have been consistently reproduced across multiple experiments.

The Skyrme model features gauge field descriptions of both electromagnetic and weak interactions, with the former requiring a non-trivial interpretation of charge conservation due to the presence of chiral anomalies. Recently, a modified Skyrme model emerged, derived from born-infinitized equations, able to accommodate an electromagnetic gauge field while dispelling concerns over conservation issues. Moreover, researchers discovered a new non-vacuum solution class within this model, characterized by both finite energy density and magnetic charge. This study aims to identify a self-dual version of this non-vacuum solution, potentially linking it to monopole-antimonopole configurations within the context of the 4D classical model. Although a fully analytical solution eludes this investigation, various approaches are explored to derive approximate expressions for such dual configurations. Firstly, a perturbative method, built on small magnetic field assumptions, yields approximate expressions for a self-dual solution, albeit with zero topological charge. Conversely, a numerical resolution utilizing a finite element method succeeds in finding a self-dual solution, albeit with negligible discrepancies when compared to approximate perturbative estimates. Finally, a gauge field reconfiguration, drawing inspiration from the 't Hooft-Polyakov solution, is found to provide an alternative perspective on these dual configurations, highlighting a potential link between these solutions and elements of nonabelian flux tube physics.

By incorporating a random magnetic field with a flux that varies in a fractal pattern, researchers have created a model that controls the formation of semi-metals using the tight-binding model on a three-dimensional hypercubic lattice. In the absence of this random magnetic field, Weyl semi-metals only occur when the flux is at specific, irregular levels. As the random magnetic field is introduced, semi-metal phases emerge at intervening integer levels of flux. The semi-metal states exhibit unique characteristics, such as broken time-reversal symmetry and highly variable carrier densities. The increase in disorder is associated with a rise in semi-metal domain sizes, observed to be significantly larger than in studies of lattice disorder. Furthermore, it has been found that the blockage of carriers within the semi-metal domains transitions from a one-dimensional to a two-dimensional pattern as the flux reaches a value of six. This is the result of a critical value of disorder, which reaches a maximum at this flux level due to the highly complex nature of the'swiss cheese' lattice structure at higher flux values.

The development of highly luminous optical sources using nanoantennas is a rapidly evolving field with numerous potential applications, yet achieving this goal remains a complex and unresolved challenge. In this study, we present a novel, hybrid optical source based on a dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna, where a central silicon nanobeam on a substrate is integrated with a coupled graphene nanotransmission line. The combination of these components yields unique capabilities, including unidirectional, strong, and luminous light emission. The novel antenna is able to efficiently convert electromagnetic power into localized light, producing a high luminosity while maintaining low back-scattering. The characteristics of the proposed antenna were thoroughly investigated using comprehensive numerical analyses. The results demonstrate that this hybrid nanoantenna meets the criteria for efficient, luminous, and unidirectional photon sources. Specifically, at a fixed input power, the novel antenna can achieve a higher emission rate and luminosity compared to previous solutions, while its low back-scattering rate remains within the "weak coupling limit" for efficient coupling with the next generation of light-matter interface systems.

Researchers have discovered a phenomenon where a force acting on a single grain within a granular assembly is partially counteracted by a dynamic system of stresses and interactions with neighboring grains. A computational model grounded in statistical mechanics has been developed to describe this phenomenon, which was initially proposed through analytical studies. To test its accuracy, researchers conducted a simulation study under controlled conditions. An innovative technique allowed for the direct measurement of stress components acting on a single grain within photoelastic granular assemblies. Both experimental and simulation results were obtained under various conditions, which were then compared with computational data obtained from the established analytical model. An excellent match between experimental, simulation, and analytical data was observed, which supports the accuracy of computational model predictions. An investigation of potential influencing factors through sensitivity analysis confirmed that our experimental results align with the theoretical findings.

Investigations of individual manganese atoms within a siliconene sheet, situated on a boron nitride surface, reveal distinct manganese-based electronic configurations. Notably, as computational intensity decreases, these computations yield comparable results, showing that the manganese atom possesses three distinct electronic states, with two being valence and one being a pentagonal state. The valence states exhibit valency of one and two, respectively, suggesting that the manganese atom behaves as a divalent or monovalent center when in certain or all double bond configurations. The pentagonal state shows characteristics of an empty molecular orbital, suggesting that the manganese center has a +3 charge in this state. The unique properties of the interaction between the manganese center and the surrounding electrons result in a combination of 100% and partially filled orbital states. The many-body perturbation theory, specifically as implemented in GW and SCGAU approximations, shows that the valence states of the manganese center exhibit a slight energy shift, describing a d-band in the coordinate space, whereas the many-body perturbation theory fails to capture the spectral feature of the pentagonal state due to its very high energy. The calculated spectra show three distinct features, corresponding to the manganese-based electronic states, positioned at 0.38 eV, 1.2 eV, and 2.6 eV, each being a spectral component, namely, the shoulder, peak, and hump, respectively, of the absorption spectrum, which can be explained by the computational many

The circular explosion that created Sgr A East, a relatively small nebula in the center of the Milky Way, is unidentified. To determine the origin of this explosion, we conducted theoretical calculations to simulate the development of different nebula models. Our research identified a specific type of explosion, known as a 15-Joule ^{56} Ni event, which accurately replicates the observed characteristics of Sgr A East. The explosion is believed to have originated from a white dwarf due to the accumulation of mass from a nearby 3-4 solar mass red supergiant star, based on our spatial density analysis. As a result, we propose that Sgr A East is the aftermath of a thermonuclear supernova that occurred within the past 15 million years. Moreover, we suggest that the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way may be surrounded by a large system of white dwarf remnant supernovae, totaling between one to five events.

This research investigates the effectiveness of seven synthetic oversampling methods three synthetic undersampling methods, and one class-specific undersampling method in a multi-class text categorization framework when the majority class is resampled using supervised and unsupervised approaches with random undersampling for the minority classes. Notably, these methods were previously evaluated solely in binary classification settings. As part of a larger experiment examining the impact of oversampling techniques, the study also assesses the performance of four different class imbalance oversampling methods, providing a comprehensive understanding of their relative effectiveness in a multi-class scenario after class imbalance relief. Moreover, the study applies a novel satellite imagery dataset, offering a practical comparison of the evaluated methods in a real-world setting where class imbalance is present. Ultimately, the findings provide insights that can inform researchers and practitioners on the best-approach to class imbalance problems in multi-class settings, which can be invaluable in practical applications where such imbalances typically occur.

This study analyses the correlation between COVID coverage in different American regions and their subsequent case and death rates, focusing on early pandemic periods. It aims to identify patterns in COVID reporting across various US areas, including both high-high and low-low correlation patterns. The research also explores possible explanations for these patterns, relates them to existing social and political divisions in the US, and investigates if similar patterns occur within international regions. The data consists of a five-category COVID coverage rating system created by combining Quantumanalytix's metrics on 200 US news sources and their associated geographic regions. The findings reveal substantial variations in COVID coverage among regional news sources, both within and outside the US. Furthermore, the research reveals a strong connection between COVID coverage in different areas and their case and death rates. In the US, regions with the highest COVID coverage tend to have the deadliest outcomes, both locally and when comparing adjacent regions. The study also finds correlations between COVID coverage and demographic variables, such as age and ethnicity, as well as political polarization. The research demonstrates that COVID-related news coverage differs based on the audience it's aimed at. The study also provides international comparisons, where regions with the highest COVID coverage in non-US areas with similar demographic characteristics tend to have the deadliest outcomes. Notably, the research finds lower COVID coverage in areas with younger populations but also highlights significant within-group variations in COVID coverage.

The Rapid Multipole Method, a technique used to calculate the short-range interaction between objects in molecular dynamics simulations, typically operates without regard to object rotation. However, this approach can cause local angular momentum fluctuations, even though the overall system remains rotationally conserved. In order to rectify this issue, it is possible to modify the algorithm by having objects, or particles, rotate in a manner that adheres to the conservation of relative angular momentum. This can be achieved by introducing a constraint that prevents the transmission of angular momentum through the use of adapted interaction operators. Furthermore, the proposed method ensures global angular momentum conservation without impacting its accuracy since the total angular momentum remains unchanged regardless of the choice of objects to be rotated. In addition to this, it is possible to maintain the accuracy of simulations even when using objects that are free to rotate by applying the method on a basis of pairs rather than individual objects.

This article provides an insight into a notable yet subtle aspect of deep-inelastic scattering where initial proton polarization partially transfers to the final proton. Calculations in both the framework of perturbation theory and using the Gell-Mann and Low method in the presence of a specific electron-proton interaction reveal some intriguing results. Despite some complexities arising from the initial state, analysis establishes that, in deep-inelastic scattering, a sizable percentage of the initial proton's polarization indeed gets transferred to the final proton. This finding is rather intriguing, given that, in other forms of scattering, such polarization transfer is not observed. Furthermore, it has been determined that the amount of polarization shift is directly linked to the square of the electron-proton potential and inversely linked to the squared momentum. At a 10 GeV laboratory energy, for instance, such polarization shift is expected to be around 0.01%, whereas at a 100 GeV laboratory energy, it would be approximately 0.0008%. This phenomenon is likely to be observable at high-energy electron-proton colliders but not at low-energy proton targets used in PS, S, or BEPC colliders. However, such polarization shift may also occur in other forms of deep-inelastic scattering involving virtual photons, with analysis suggesting that, in such cases, a sizable percentage of the polarization should be retained in the final antiproton at a certain stage of Minkowskian energy.

In a scenario where a network has access to a small amount of training data from an expert source, we're exploring approaches to augment this data by leveraging additional information, such as prior knowledge or network collaborations. The goal is to develop training methods that allow a neural network to learn efficiently from these external sources. Previous research demonstrated that a specific type of data augmentation, when applied to an ensemble of networks, could increase the robustness and efficiency of their collective decisions. This work builds on that concept and develops a new method that directly enhances decision-making confidence through augmentation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed approach can significantly boost the performance of a single neural network when trained with augmented versions of its own predictions, even in the absence of external experts. Ultimately, we evaluate our method's effectiveness using human-labeled datasets within the realm of medical image analysis, and compare its capabilities with existing approaches.

A comprehensive study of vector boson pair production, primarily consisting of W and Z bosons, in the presence of a Higgs boson (in its ZZ and ZZ modes) that decays into $b\bar{b}$ or $\ell\ell$ ($\ell$ denoting electrons or muons), has been carried out using 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at 13 TeV by the ATLAS experiment. Vector boson pair signals were evaluated against a diverse set of background processes featuring jets, gamma rays, and non-perturbative phenomena. None of the analyzed signal scenarios, encompassing both charged and neutral vector bosons decaying into leptons or bottom quarks, aligned with observed data congruence, thereby setting stringent limits on charged vector boson production, particularly in relation to $\mathrm{W}^\pm Z$ scenarios. Furthermore, the study presents the most precise measurements of Z boson transverse momentum in the presence of a Higgs boson (in its $\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{Z}^\ast) \rightarrow \ell\ell \ell\ell$ state) and the Higgs boson itself since its discovery, along with constraints on charged Higgs boson properties under two anomaly models, thus offering insights into potential issues with electroweak symmetry breakdown predictions in these scenarios.

The development of solid-state lasers has been pivotal in astronomy and space exploration, with numerous applications still unfolding. A novel concept for an electronic-based alkali-sodium laser has been devised, incorporating aspects of gas lasers and semiconductor devices. This innovative approach enables the creation of compact, efficient, and coherent light sources with broad bandwidths, encompassing the near infrared to visible spectral regions. This strategy may facilitate the design of solid-state lasers capable of operating stably at elevated temperatures, thus allowing for planetary missions and other space-based applications.

We establish that two K3 varieties in the vicinity of a Prym variety, after adjusting their complex structures via period map values, can be observed approaching but not reaching each other. This achievement is achieved through a four-dimensional hyperbolic cusp form with a specified frequency and a previously established bound on the Hecke eigenvalues of this form. This result also has a byproduct implication regarding Siegel disks of complex multiplication K3 varieties, yielding a classification of their locations based on the 10-parameter Holonomy group.

Within the framework of the supersymmetric SO(10) model, we explore the concept of dark matter which is embodied by the neutralino's degradation. Utilizing SO(10) model based on the gauge group $SU(5)_{C} \otimes SU(5)_{H}$ decomposition, and considering a minimal set of soft supersymmetry-breaking terms with a high-scale $A$-term, the neutralino is identified as the lightest particle and is composed of several components. As a result, its mass is determined to be approximately $1200$ GeV and is subject to decay processes. Even in the event that its mass is greater than $1200$ GeV, its low-value $A$, along with the related parameters, allows for a manageable value of its mass through the influence of the left-handed neutrino dark matter hypothesis, and thus its decay into more stable particles can occur at a later stage. Furthermore, this decay process modulates the neutralino's initial dark matter distribution such that its earlier distribution becomes concentrated within larger mass regions and, in the event of the neutralino's mass being greater than $1200$ GHz, its distribution becomes concentrated within smaller mass regions. In this study, we also calculate the neutrino dark matter annihilation signal and its associated gamma radiation spectrum within the context of SO(10) model based on the gauge group $SU(5)_{C} \otimes SU(5)_{H}$ decomposition.

The genus of a graph G, denoted by γ(G), is the minimum number of planes needed to embed G such that no edges intersect. In 1966, Moon made the conjecture that a graph with n vertices and degree d should have its genus bounded by a polynomial of n and d, which was later confirmed by Kahn and Savitch in 1989. They also showed that γ(G) is bounded by a polynomial of n and 1/d^2. Our research provides a new effective polynomial-time algorithm to approximate γ(G) with input parameters n and d. The algorithm works by first estimating the genus of each connected component of G using a polynomial that depends on the component's order (n_c) and the maximum degree of its vertices (Δ), which we previously developed. These estimates can be calculated in total polynomial time since we consider the parameters n and d fixed. Next, the algorithm sums up the estimated genera of all connected components of G. Since our previous polynomial bound for the genus of a single component in terms of n_c and Δ does not directly apply to the case where d varies between n_c and 1, we first convert the relevant part of the exponent into a term that depends on the square of d. Our modified polynomial can then be applied to derive an upper bound for the genus of a graph with n vertices and degree d. The new bound depends on n and the square of d, which confirms Moon's originally proposed relationship. Our method for approx

This paper presents a decentralized algorithm for solving a convex optimization problem that has a differentiable, strongly convex, and continuously differentiable gradient within a closed-form. The algorithm, an optimized iteration of previous research via A. R. Teixeira, et al., is a communication-efficient solution that requires the transfer of a single gradient update per iteration and can be strongly convergent in a network with a connected topology. We analyze the algorithm's convergence, speed, and stability by using Lyapunov's method and a stochastic analysis. Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm achieves faster convergence rates for a strongly convex function and similar convergence rates with noise as other methods, while also ensuring the stability of the algorithm in the presence of relaxed assumptions. Furthermore, we compare the algorithm's performance using a realistic traffic model, demonstrating that it results in comparable convergence rates with less frequent message passing compared to other methods, such as D-PCA and NED-PCA.

This study focuses on developing hate-speech detection systems for two predominantly hate speech-targeting demographics in India: Hindus and Muslims. Utilizing publicly available datasets from social media platforms, such as Twitter, we create training and testing corpora in Hindi and Bengali, and employ transfer learning with pre-existing neural network models to achieve high-precision results. Furthermore, we devise and train a series of neural networks using the same objectives as well as a novel feature-rich model, leveraging the word-subword embedding system WordPiece, to explore enhanced performance and theoretical implications. By leveraging the substantial amounts of low-resource data available in India's indigenous languages, we demonstrate the efficacy of hate-speech detection systems powered by transfer learning, and propose possible future research directions.

In particle detectors, especially those like MicroBooNE using Low Energy Ionization detectors in a neutrino experiment, detecting the movement of ions due to particle collisions is crucial for identifying those collisions. While it's possible that the ions are completely removed from the detector using their initial velocities, it's not always the case. Some collisions may cause ions to change direction without being expelled from the detector, while others may knock them out of the detector altogether. Traditional analysis techniques may not be able to distinguish between these different types of collisions, leading to incorrect conclusions about the results. However, there are alternative analysis techniques, like those based on the "recoil invariant mass" or "impact parameter" concepts, that are able to identify the different types of collisions and their effects on the ions. This study examines the accuracy and usability of these different analysis techniques using different types of events, including those where the ions are only slightly changed direction, others where the ions are completely expelled from the detector, and yet others where the ions are actually released from the detector but then bounce back off the edge. The techniques prove to be reliable and accurate, and the concepts are now applied to real-world data from a MicroBooNE experiment.

This study incorporates the expertise of behavioral scientists to create a more comprehensive system for evaluating the impact of commercial information on safe driving. Our framework builds upon the existing DriverChoice platform, which enables the comparison of various information formats in terms of safety and utility. The driver's decision-making process is recorded, including their motivations for actions taken, which are then evaluated by contextual analysis to assess safety and utility. This approach allows for the accurate assessment of commercial information on real-world driving behaviors while considering actual driving conditions. To illustrate the benefits of our framework, a preference elicitation study was conducted in which drivers navigated scenarios with misleading COP warnings on GPS maps. Our findings showed that drivers who received these warnings had lower utility and safety compared to those who did not receive them, ultimately leading to a significant number of accidents. Our study highlights the value of our framework in supporting the development of commercial driving safety protocols by evaluating the direct consequences of various actions in real-world driving scenarios.

The NeurIPS 2021 task is the third out-of-context benchmark. The challenge involves reassembling and re-ranking previously generated candidate phrases to form new sentences that match current context. The proposed solutions include applying a soft ruler and leveraging word co-occurrence frequencies. The top model employs transformer-based self-attention to guide re-ranking, whereas the secondary approach utilizes linear probing of pre-trained language models to determine the quality of candidate sentences. The combination of the two methods achieves the best performance, securing first place in out-of-context benchmark evaluations. The experiment results indicate that our method excels in both automatic and human evaluation scores.

Determining optimal navigation rules for a navigator with incomplete information on its environment and the locations of all navigators within it is a major research aim, with solutions potentially providing a foundation for the creation of multi-agent coordination strategies. Existing theories on optimal navigation rules include the Page-Equilibrium protocol and the Bayesian training of neural networks by which the navigators adjust their movement speeds to minimize their expected time to reach designated destinations within the environment. A linear Gaussian stochastic process model has been developed to analyze the navigation rules with the most optimal times, resulting in a geometric interpretation where a specific navigation path can be represented as a geodesic curve within a multidimensional Gaussian stochastic field manifold. By applying a specific mathematical criterion, it has been possible to identify the shortest paths between two points in a Gaussian stochastic process.

This note provides a straightforward demonstration of the previously reported phenomenon of periodic film thickness variation in thin films deposited using pulsed ion sputtering.  Prolonged deposition using a pulsed DC sputtering system, unattended and interrupted only by power outages, has been found to yield a film growth profile that displays periodic thickness fluctuations.  The emergence of these thickness fluctuations is attributed to an intermittent power supply, which exhibits periodic power availability.  The study presents an alternative, yet simplified, method for observing the periodic behavior of thin films deposited via pulsed ion sputtering.  It is anticipated that this contribution will provide valuable insights for researchers conducting experiments using pulsed ion sputtering, particularly those working without automated systems.

This investigation centers on an infinite series of L-functions associated with a family of cuspidal automorphic representations that have a weight of 2 and are part of the GL2(A_ℝ) symmetrical group. We identify a novel pattern in the unique values of these L-functions at critical points, denoted as Λ(σ, f) = P(σ, f) + (2i)^(k-1)N(σ, f), where the polynomial component P(σ, f) and neatness function N(σ, f) can be precisely defined using the family's representation and are known to remain bounded for any given real number σ. Furthermore, these newly discovered functions, P(σ, f) and N(σ, f), exhibit various mathematical benefits, and the study connects them to a link between the values of these L-functions and the patterns in the modular world, specifically the Ramanujan-Sato-Serre conjecture, which posits that for any given modular form, the number of its Fourier coefficients should not exceed the bound of 2+ε. This investigation presents a partial verification of this conjecture, which aligns with recent findings by Mukta, Naijan, Chareng, Preeaipan, Rukku, Suresh, Veeraraghava and Yogesh.

We employed magnetic impedance mapping to study spin-dependent transport in graphene nanostructures, leveraging its invariance under electron spin and orientation. This capability allowed us to investigate how magnetization influences current flow in vertical graphene nanorings and identical rings with a head-to-tail magnetic arrangement. Furthermore, we analyzed the transport properties of irregular magnetic loops, comparing them to their non-magnetic counterparts. Impedance mapping also facilitated the identification of contact points between leads and graphene in scanning tunneling microscopy images, and we explored the spin-dependent conductance of parallel and anti-parallel magnetized graphene nanotubes.

We establish theorems that allow us to assess the convergence of certain nonlinear approximation methods applied to non-linear weakly monotonic operators acting on function spaces. Our findings specifically pertain to the weakly nonlinear operator defined by $T_{\sigma,\delta}(x)(t) = \frac{\sigma x(t)+\delta}{\delta}$. Notably, this operator falls short of being Lipschitz on any finite interval. Our results also address the convergence of two other types of nonlinear approximation methods, namely the first being the Adomian algorithm which utilizes the series form $Ad(x)(\lambda,\delta,\sigma) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}u_n$, and secondly the Decomposition Method which generates the series $DM(x)$, both associated with the differential equation $u_{tt}=u_{xx}_t=t$. Our results reveal that the approximation series produced by these methods converge to the exact solution under the condition that the approximation is performed on an extended space. Our theorems, which cover a range of nonlinear approximation methods applied to nonlinear operators, provide a Korovkin-style theorem for approximation theory. Our approximation results were confirmed using the Korovkin theorem, a convergence theorem for sequences of linear operators that guarantees their convergence under certain conditions.

The concept of pancyclicity is crucial in graph theory, enabling a graph to contain a cycle connecting every pair of vertices. A connected graph possessing pancyclicity is therefore able to allow a cycle that connects every vertex of the graph. In this study, a new class of graphs called generalised irregular graphs is introduced, characterised by certain conditions and properties. Results showing the relationship between pancyclicity, autonomy number, and Hamiltonicity in these graphs are demonstrated, with specific conditions such as the degree and size of the graphs being taken into account. Our evidence supports the possibility that a particular condition can lead to pancyclicity. Finally, a method to construct large irregular graphs is provided, with specific examples of pancyclic graphs derived from this construction.

Our research examines the directed flow of various hadrons in heavy ion collisions, including Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and a unique study on isobar collisions with specific charges. We analyzed data from the PHENIX and STAR experiments, comparing it to a theoretical model that incorporates the effects of a global entropy gradient, as well as a hypothetical QCD critical point. By assuming that hadrons follow the Coherent Energy Density Sample (CEDS) model, our findings show that the directed flow of both light and strange hadrons can be described, considering a scenario with no quark composition. However, when including quarks, our model struggles to perfectly replicate the flow of more complex particles like oxides and certain baryons. We also studied the directed flow of strange hadrons in a specific time frame and discovered that its behavior could indicate the presence of a complex strangeness dependence if the directed flow behaved differently depending on strangeness signs. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the directed flow of all the studied hadrons crosses to negative values at high rapidity, exhibiting dN/dη ~ 1, except for π° and K° where this value remains positive at high rapidity. Isobar collision data was also investigated and showed that the directed flow of positive and negative hadrons has distinct behaviors depending on the color electric field created in these specific collisions.

The adaptive spectral Koopman technique offers a novel method for dynamic system analysis with only partial knowledge of the system's initial conditions. It's particularly effective for low-dimensional systems lacking simple, closed-form representations, but it suffers from computational efficiency issues due to the high cost of quadrature methods used to evaluate system data. To resolve these challenges, the proposed research integrates sparse grid techniques into the adaptive spectral Koopman approach, significantly boosting computational speed while maintaining precision. It's demonstrated that the hybrid method can successfully identify key state variables in a knowing-glass-box environment and distill complex, multi-variable time-series data into their fundamental components. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is tested on a complex system model before being used to investigate the dynamics of a nonlinear pendulum system, where it accurately predicts the frequency of wobble movements, even when some data points are excluded from the analysis.

This article outlines the theoretical foundation for applying the outward complex scaling technique to solve the Schrödinger equation for an atom or molecule in a strong electric field. The approach relies on a $p$-hyperbolic potential, a function that increases in complexity with $p$, to determine scaling factors. A comprehensive review of the method's underlying principles is provided, including its adaptation to systems with multiple nuclei and the strategies for distinguishing continuum and bounded states. Several examples are examined, such as the crossroads in Be+ caused by the Vaubel-Stump automatic crossing, to demonstrate the efficacy of the outward complex scaling technique. However, concerns are raised regarding potential errors in computing dipole stabilization energies due to the inability to accurately determine scaling parameters for bounded states, as evidenced by comparisons of the orbital stabilization effect in He and Xe$^{2+}$.

We demonstrate that the Sinkhorn algorithm does not converge when the associated Jacobians are not surjective, at least under the condition specified in Moser and Rudin's counterexample. We show this by constructing a specific transportation problem where the algorithm diverges and show further that a generalized version of this problem shares a key property with Moser and Rudin's example: it is not resolved through iterated projections.

Measurements of total and differential cross-sections are presented for pairs of top and anti-top quarks produced in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV with the ATLAS detector at the LHC, based on data with an integrated luminosity of 257 pb^-1. Dilepton, leptonic and semi-leptonic decay modes of the top quarks are considered, and the differential cross-sections are calculated in bins of charged particle multiplicity and transverse momentum. These measurements, made in the pseudorapidity range |η| < 2.9 for the tagged top quark and |η| < 2.0 for the reconstructed anti-top quark, cover the transverse momentum range up to 120 GeV for the tagged top quark and up to 200 GeV for the reconstructed anti-top quark. The data, based on more than 159 signal events, is presented in the total t¯t cross-section scenario and compared with state-of-the-art perturbative QCD calculations, with a notable agreement between the two. Additionally, the t¯t cross-section of approximately 43.5 ± 3.3 (stat.) ± 3.1 (syst.) ± 3.1 (exp.) ± 2.9 (theory) pb has been determined, with an experimental uncertainty dominated by acceptance and luminosity corrections for the first time using data from proton-nucleus collisions, and validating the theoretical prediction

This study focuses on the localization phenomenon in a complex network with a central hub, using an agent-based model and code simulation. Results indicate that the extent of localization is determined by the network's layout, specifically the connections leading out of the central node. When those connections are diversified, the resulting localization is spread out and efficient, but this does not automatically lead to enhanced robustness in the event of the central node's failure. Furthermore, in this system we have identified conditions that cause the spread of an epidemic to be lower when the central node is removed, as opposed to a randomized system with an equivalent level of connectivity.

The geometric characteristics of a star-like function are associated with its classification within the Janowski class, denoted by $J(a,b,c)$. This paper explores the relationship between $J(a,b,c)$ and the function's distance to convexity, with a focus on identifying new distance to convexity bounds. To achieve this, we introduce the generalised modified second type Bessel function, $I_{\alpha}(z)$, and use its convex form to express even and odd functions, $e_{\alpha}(z)$, which are derived from $I_{\alpha}(z)$. These functions are then linked to the classification of $J(a,b,c)$ via its distance to convexity, with the distance parameter $\alpha$ determining whether $e_{\alpha}(z)$ falls within the Janowski or Stieltjes class. This approach allows for the recovery of known results and the generation of four novel bounds on distance to convexity.

This study examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on urban mobility patterns in fifty urban centers around the world. By using mobile device data, we find that the pandemic led to a dramatic shift in the movement habits of the affluent, with a reduced likelihood of visiting multiple locations within a single trip, or'multi-stop behavior.' In contrast, the lower-income population continued to exhibit pre-pandemic multi-stop behavior, resulting in a notable disparity in movement patterns between high and low-income individuals. Furthermore, to better comprehend these differences, we employ a discrete choice model, linking the choices made by individuals to their respective socioeconomic characteristics. The analysis suggests that the significant changes in urban mobility patterns during the pandemic primarily stem from the varied financial resources and risk perceptions unique to each demographic. By highlighting the complex influences of socioeconomic factors on urban mobility patterns, the findings present valuable insights for developing targeted urban mobility policies that incorporate a multi-stop strategy.

The success of numerical simulations for two-phase flow in complex porous media relies heavily on the accuracy of precomputered data, specifically fine-scale reservoir rock and flow characteristics. Creating such preconditions involves solving nonlinear partial differential equations, which can be computationally costly, even when using numerical methods that converge rapidly. Field-split preconditioning offers an alternative approach by allowing for the use of slower-converging but cheaper subproblems at each iteration, while still achieving convergence through outer solver iterations. This paper presents four distinct nonlinear field-split preconditioners, tested on synthetic models mimicking real-world uneven porous media structures, with comparisons showing that these approaches can lead to significant improvements in computational efficiency. Yet, it's anticipated that the actual implementation in larger-scale realistic models will uncover additional challenges. Hence, a comprehensive evaluation of these techniques in more realistic scenarios will be crucial for their optimal performance.

The combination of optical cavities and circularly rotating light is foundational to chiral photonics, offering opportunities for advanced research. A new proposal has been put forward, suggesting that this concept can be taken in a different direction by using an optical cavity in a setting where the rules of mirror symmetry no longer apply. This would involve the cavity's mirrors not being perfectly symmetrical, allowing for two distinct optical states: one where the rules of chirality apply, and another where they do not. A possible way to achieve this system has been proposed, based on using artificial magnetic surfaces and controlled light inputs. Simulations indicate that by fine-tuning these inputs, the system can be made to operate in the proposed mode, for both microwave and optical frequencies. This breakthrough could open up a range of new applications, including the creation of new types of chiral lasers, and hold the potential to greatly expand our understanding of chiral physics in photonics.

We re-examine the relationship between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and one-loop raised Liouville CFT, with distinct emphasis on the former's role in generating the latter's central charge, driving us to re-evaluate the relevant semi-classical solutions and their boundary conditions. These semi-classical solutions are, in fact, obtained by conformally embedding flat spaces into hyperbolic spaces and imposing specific boundary conditions on the embedding functions, an observation that leads us to conjecture that only Liouville CFT emerges as the worldsheet theory of gravity solutions possessing a universal lower bound on their action, a property we dub "action lower bound conjecture". To validate this conjecture, we employ the matrix model solution of the gravity theory, with the result that the conjecture is supported by the brane interpretation of the quantum double duality conjecture, an outcome that is seemingly consistent.

A novel cosmological approach has been developed for the classic warp drive solution, incorporating the cosmological constant and based on fundamental observations of an expanding universe. The general algebraic structure of these solutions, under the constraint of steady-state momentum, is outlined, and specific examples are presented for solutions characterized by zero and negative cosmological constants. Notably, solutions with a negative cosmological constant and pure momentum yield a spacetime geometry similar to an expanding de Sitter universe, featuring a spacelike singularity and an event horizon, and the specific values of the singularity and horizon can be determined quantitatively. Crucially, the derived solutions satisfy Einstein's field equations for an expanding universe, match the fundamental principles of general relativity and quantum mechanics, and the specific geometry of the spacetime can be manipulated by adjusting the warp drive's engine.

As cities' infrastructures shift towards smart and sustainable systems, their foundation relies on efficient urban planning. Effective planning requires comprehensive geographic information, but existing systems often face obstacles such as inadequate data integration, inefficient search functions, and an absence of user-friendly interfaces. To address these issues, the GUIDES project was implemented, providing data engineering solutions for searching and visualizing city planning data across various platforms, including databases, web applications, and data visualization tools. By combining city planning data and geographic information frameworks, the GUIDES project enables developers and cities to seamlessly store, manage, and display urban data, thereby streamlining search and visualization processes. The project encompasses a range of innovations, encompassing a content-addressable database, web services, and interactive visualization, designed to facilitate data retrieval and display. The GUIDES project comprises a scalable and adaptable suite of tools for building custom city planning data applications, as demonstrated by its implementation in the cities of Aachen and Berlin.

To study the behavior of individual emitters in a highly ordered two-dimensional penumbral crystal, we utilize optical resonance between the emitters and a central laser beam, enabling us to investigate the crystal's dynamics with high resolution. By analyzing the resulting resonance pattern, we can determine the level of random movement among the emitters, which corresponds to specific values of momentum. Our approach allows us to identify individual emitters, their individual modes of movement, and the rate at which they are being heated. Furthermore, we can utilize this technique to gather information about the initial and current states of the crystal's motion. By making comparisons between the behavior of crystals trapped near an electric field and those under the influence of a magnetic field, we can illustrate that the former experiences increased levels of dephasing due to the electric field's higher effectiveness in transferring energy to the emitters.

A new approach integrating quantum mechanics for light emitted by molecules in Near Field Scattering is presented. This approach takes into consideration the interactions between a molecule and electromagnetic fields, as well as the strong electrical signals produced in Tip-Enhanced Raman Scattering (TERS). We evaluated a specific TERS setup with a silver tip and tip-enhanced localized plasmons, and found that molecular orientation has a significant impact on both the emitted light frequency and intensity. This confirms that quantum mechanical simulations as complex as electron motion within molecules and spin-orbit coupling are necessary for accurate simulations. However, such simulations remain challenging due to computational complexity. Therefore, a simpler method using classical mechanical equations to model light frequency and a quantum mechanical model using a two-level approximation for electron excitation, is proposed and found to be effective in matching the results of more complex simulations in both single and two-photon TERS cases. This proposed method could significantly reduce the required level of computational complexity by using present-day algorithms, making it more feasible to apply to various TERS systems and molecules.

We conducted K-band observations of seven galaxies, including the Milky Way's center, the radio galaxy Cen A, and five nearby non-active spiral galaxies, using the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope. Our goal was to analyze these galaxies for low-intensity radio emission analogous to the phenomenon of Fast Radio Bursts. The galaxies' right ascensions were purposefully selected to include fast-swinging radio source J0348-2741, known for repeating Fast Radio Bursts, to increase the detection efficiency. The data collection took place over three observing sessions in 2020, covering a frequency range from 20 to 26 GHz. By combining the frequencies and applying a mode-matching technique, we processed the data to a bandwidth of 3 GHz. The resulting spectra of the galaxies did not exhibit any sharp structures like Fast Radio Bursts, but rather showed only continuous and flat microwave background noise. The data of J0348-2741 did not reveal any new and significant radio emission, nor did we detect unusual radio emission in the observed non-active galaxies. Our analysis of the Sardinia Radio Telescope's sensitivity indicated a detection threshold of about 12 Jy for a single pulse of a Fast Radio Burst, however this does not exclude the possibility of detecting lower-level microwave excess, possibly related to previously known radio emission, in the observed galaxies. By applying the Parkes survey method, we set an upper limit to any unpolarized emission of less than 0.000

The entropic changes displayed by ammonium sulfate's molecular, ferroelectric, and caloric properties are considered considerable and are caused by the relatively small size of the alteration in its enthalpy and entropy changes. In particular, the molecular solid's enthalpy and entropy changes during its phase transition amount to only 0.76 kT and 1.03 kT, respectively. We found that the source of these substantial entropic changes stems from the transfer of phonon entropy from the Pioneer state, found in low-temperature (PT) states, to the Larmor state, represented as $\Lambda$. The Pioneer state boasts an abundance of phonon configurations characterized by 4, 6, and 8 molecule rings, whereas the Larmor state is characterized by 2 molecule dipoles. The Larmor state, being less dynamic, is unable to accommodate these phonon configurations, thereby accounting for the solid's extensive entropy changes through the phonon caloric effect. This effect is attributed to the varying vibrational frequencies of the molecules in the Larmor state, spanning from 20 to 120 meV (0.53 to 3.15 eV), signifying a polymorphic behavior. The observed phenomenon is considered a first-in-class third-order polymorphic effect (TOPE).

During reinforcement learning, agents adjust their behavior based on the comparison between anticipated and actual outcomes. Failing to accurately forecast outcomes can disrupt this adjustment process, hindering agents from learning from their experiences. Two proposed methods for addressing this problem, reward lumping and epochizing, involve modifying the way agents process feedback, either by aggregating multiple events or by dividing trials into fixed segments, both leading to improved agent performance. Our study discovered that these agents, characterized by their agents either processing feedback cumulatively or separately, exhibit distinct midbrain activity patterns, specifically in the dorsolateral and shell regions of the substantia nigra, where their activity differentiates when outcomes are unexpected. This distinction suggests that these agents' success is linked to their unique strategies for processing feedback, particularly in how they respond to unexpected outcomes. Our findings imply that both lumping and epochizing strategies could enhance reinforcement learning by mitigating the adverse effects of failed predictions.

This study, conducted by international researchers Gomis, Laliena and Sánchez, presents a novel class of interpolations for several $E_8$ lattice models that were originally quantum in nature, now becoming non-quantum due to complexification. They explore this phenomenon, highlighting its impact on entanglement and quantum contextuality, utilizing two specific metrics: the von Neumann entropy for entanglement and the IQHD theory for contextuality with $E_8$ lattice interpolations of dimensions 4 and 8. Their analysis reveals that no quantum entanglement exists in the 4D interpolation, while non-quantum entanglement emerges in the 8D interpolation, both cases being highly complex. Contrasting the behavior of the 8D quantum and non-quantum systems, the researchers find that quantum contextuality is present in the former but absent in the latter. Most surprisingly, the quantum regime of the 8D system exhibits no signs of quantum entanglement. Their results have significant implications for further research on entanglement and contextuality in complex lattice models, while also shedding light on complexifications that may have been overlooked in previous studies.

We employ the Frechet distance to analyze the close neighbor problem for time series, where the objective is to pinpoint all time series within a specified maximum distance threshold to a query time series. Initially, a lower bound exists for the number of necessary comparisons in the general case; subsequent work has established both a maximum limit for searching over ordered, non-overlapping sub-intervals and a bounded range limit with known constants. In this study, another lower bound was established for the number of necessary comparisons, specifically for the case where searching over ordered, non-overlapping sub-intervals can be executed. Our analysis reveals that for m time series, the minimum number of comparisons required does not exceed (m + 2) log(m). Furthermore, we demonstrate that for the case where searching over ordered, non-overlapping sub-intervals is efficiently executed with k comparisons, the bounded range limit is constrained by the formula (k-1)(m-1 + 2log(m)). Both the established lower bound and the bounded range limit with the previously found constant of 4 can be verified to be optimal solutions for n = (m-1) data points. Our work solves the open problem from 2019 by proving that for the case where searching over ordered, non-overlapping sub-intervals is efficiently executed with k comparisons, the bounded range limit is constrained by the formula (k-1)m.

High-precision experiments are frequently hindered by measurement uncertainty. This work introduces a novel strategy known as iterative Bayesian unraveling to enhance precision, particularly effective in experiments using continuous variables. The method is demonstrated through the application of reducing measurement error in the measurement of two-field Pauli states. The proposed strategy offers significant advantages in the following ways. Firstly, it enables the effective use of incomplete data, thereby overcoming the limitation of having no explicit wavefunctions. Secondly, it allows for the reduction of measurement uncertainty even when the actual wavefunction is distorted. Lastly, iterative Bayesian unraveling can facilitate the projection of an arbitrary initial superposition into a nearby target state, thereby serving as an effective tool for state preparation.

Humans have traditionally communicated intentions through nonverbal signals like facial expressions, body language, and vocal inflections. As people interact with an increasing number of intelligent systems, communicating intentions remains an essential challenge. In field studies, our team found that humans working alongside robots often use subtle behavioral cues such as eye gaze, gestures, and physical proximity to convey their intentions. In one instance, a participant utilized a 'helpful nudge' to guide a struggling robot to complete a task. Conversely, other nudge attempts from humans aimed at assisting the robot were thwarted because the intent was misinterpreted as an intrusive action. Observing these shared autonomy scenarios, our hypothesis is that incorporating expressions of intent through eye gestures, body language, and spatial engagement between humans and robots can streamline interactions and enhance user experience. In experiments conducted with a conveying robot via shared autonomy, our data demonstrates that a higher percentage of participants preferred the intent-explicit model over a baseline system (64\% vs. 52\%), in addition to faster completion times and greater participant engagement.

There's a pressing need for safety in automated systems operating in unfamiliar environments. Developing algorithms that prevent collisions between robots and sensors is crucial, and task-oriented collision risk management is a promising approach. Current methods estimate environments using maps and predict the paths of objects based on these estimates. However, in unfamiliar settings, these estimations can be incorrect, making reliable risk assessment and collision prevention challenging. To address this issue, we present a novel risk assessment framework that leverages a new type of map called HiTMap, which employs a combination of abstract spatial representations and location-specific maps. By combining these, HiTMap accurately detects when an object is about to leave a defined area. Compared to existing temporary data structures, HiTMap's benefits are retained even after the initial data is removed, and it outperforms other methods in testing on a mobile robot navigating through the University of Texas at Austin campus, demonstrating a 33% reduction in computation compared to other methods, and nearly a 10-fold improvement in processing time after the data has been removed.

This paper contributes two novel digital sequences: the inter-group supplementary sequence and the 2-D Z-complementary array code sequence. The inter-group supplementary sequence is designed to incorporate two distinct digital sequences, allowing for the creation of two incompatible group codes from a single code framework. Meanwhile, the 2-D Z-complementary array code sequence is formed by two incompatible 2-D codes that share a common code index, yet exhibit zero summation when any row and column are selected. Notably, these two new sequences draw on the concept of multivariable functions, specifically as a solution to the problem of incomplete combinatorial mathematics. Furthermore, these novel sequences can generate respective encoding matrices with large minimum weights, demonstrating their potential applicability and utility.

A new variational framework is created for simultaneous reconstruction of images from multiple energy levels, noise reduction, and material separation in X-Ray Computed Tomography (CT) scans. The traditional inverse radon transform formula is used to calculate the CT projections, with the assumptions that the object's material density gradually changes and the attenuation coefficients follow the Coulomb-Born model. The proposed method uses four-level Coulomb series (two types of photons and two reflections) to improve the reconstruction process. Non-Gaussian noise is described by a Weibull distribution, with the scale parameter varying across the image. Three distinct models are considered for material separation, each with their own objective functions. The framework minimizes a total energy functional, with a weighted sum of image gradients, separating terms, and noise estimation terms. The method uses fast fourier transforms and a semi-implicit scheme for resolution and numerical analysis. The approach's effectiveness is validated using numerical and real-world experiments.

We investigate how electron "spillover" and nonlocal behavior influence the physics of gap-plasmons by examining the plasmonic modes that arise in superconducting nanowires and rings in the context of ultra-clean, mesoscale systems. Our analysis, which incorporates both a refined and simplified version of the density functional theory, takes into account the electron "spillover" and nonlocal behavior, in addition to electron capacitance and the screening via fermionic excitations, and highlights the inherent continuum nature of plasmons in systems with reduced gaps. By considering various scenarios, such as a nanowire and rings with diminishing gaps, our results demonstrate a deeper understanding of plasmons and the electron "spillover", and highlight the relationship between electron "spillover" and nonlocal behavior, and gap size. In the context of ultra-clean metals and in the absence of a gap, our analysis reveals a deeper relationship between electron "spillover" and nonlocal behavior, and gap size, and demonstrates the inherent nonlocality of plasmons in a mesoscale system.

Context-based name extraction technology is crucial for swiftly scanning through vast amounts of text to pinpoint significant entities, saving users from having to manually read the entire content. However, current contextual name extraction methods consistently remove too many true positive sentences from the context, leading to a significant loss of information. In an effort to mitigate this issue, this research presents a new approach called Term Significance Feedback (TSF), which utilizes a neural network to predict the importance of individual terms within a context, thereby refining the context and reducing false positives. We conduct a comprehensive performance evaluation of TSF on six diverse scientific domains, comparing it to four contemporary context-based name extraction methods. According to the evaluation results, TSF successfully reduces false positives by 30.6-61.5%, outperforms the compared methods by 10.0-41.7% in true positive rate, and maintains a relatively stable recall reduction of false negatives. Notably, TSF's success is largely due to its unique ability to provide Term Importance Vectors (TIVs) that are highly interpretable. We further illustrate that by adjusting the context using either a human or automated method, it is possible to acquire a context that yields a high TSF score, thereby validating the feedback's effectiveness. Lastly, we showcase TSF's potential to improve the retrieval from academic databases of multiple target entities by stacking the context prediction and section selection processes.

This paper emulates a study where participants assess multivariate healthcare time series for about 50 patients on a large screen, making it a challenging task. To address this, we highlight key design principles for visualizing long-term data and optimizing interactions on large, informative displays. Our proposed methods include classifying patients in real-time using three color codes (green, yellow, and red) to swiftly convey signals and allow for efficient selection of individual patients. The design also enables seamless zooming and detailed views, accessible with a single click. Our findings emphasize the significance of designing clear interactions that balance exploration and in-depth analysis, and our proposed methods can serve as a baseline for future research on multivariate time series exploration.

The vast resources of electronic health records contain valuable information for healthcare system improvement, yet analyzing these records poses significant technical challenges due to their complex structure, scalability issue, and highly encrypted content. Researchers have recently proposed new computing frameworks to extract meaningful insights from EHR data, including both structured EHR graphs and unstructured document graphs. However, these frameworks primarily focus on single EHR documents or limited clinical relationships within them. To address this limitation, I developed a global EHR graph analysis method called Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network that extracts clinical insights from extensive clinical datasets by utilizing similar EHR documents for feature representation. This pipeline composes similarity graph neural network modules, where each module analyzes a single EHR document by gathering clinical insights from three associated views: a document graph, a patient graph, and additional clinical records. This method effectively captures diverse clinical insights from EHR documents. I evaluated the pipeline by comparing its performance with existing state-of-the-art graph neural networks on two clinical classification tasks, patient similarity calculation, and disease diagnosis. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed pipeline outperforms the best existing graph neural network model, achieving up to a 2.1% improvement in AUC for patient similarity calculation and approximately 10% in F1 score for both in-hospital mortality and COVID-19 diagnosis. These findings suggest that the proposed pipeline successfully utilizes similar EHR documents to provide significant clinical insights that surpass the performance of the best existing graph neural network model.

Within a soft-matter framework, an asymmetric double layer formed at the interface of a charged flexible material and an ionic solution is examined. By incorporating the effects of solvent polarization through a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, analytical expressions are derived for the interfacial charge density, electrostatic potential, and solvent density. Moreover, the relationship between solvent density and distance from the interface is developed, taking into account the impact of flexibility and charge distribution within the flexible material. Our analysis shows that solvent polarization significantly affects the electric double layer, particularly at lower flexibility levels. This results in increased interfacial charge and a more pronounced electrostatic interaction at smaller distances from the interface. Furthermore, the unique structure of the electric double layer near highly charged deformable materials gives rise to distinct solvent density patterns. At higher deformation levels, the solvent density exhibits a double-peak pattern, characterized by a well-defined inner minimum. These findings provide valuable insights into the electric double layer at charged soft materials and can be extended to other areas of soft-matter and bio-electrochemistry research.

During software development, developers create text comments to explain their code's purpose, constraints, and behavior. In the post-development stage, requirements engineers analyze these comments to gather information about the system's original needs and use it to create specifications. Unfortunately, existing methods for extracting information from comments are inefficient and rely heavily on human input. In this work, we introduce a groundbreaking, fully automated approach that leverages deep learning to extract software specifications from a large body of unstructured text comments. Our novel method is unique because it bypasses the need for manual categorization, metadata, or domain expertise, making it scalable for large projects. We manually created specifications and comment datasets for two systems, and evaluated our approach against a baseline model, demonstrating its effectiveness in correctly predicting specifications for new, unseen systems.

This research investigates how to improve energy efficiency in networks using cooperative relay technology and network coding. We analyze a general model of a multi-user, multi-cast network, setting a goal of minimizing energy consumption by optimizing power levels at original nodes, intermediate relays, and receiving nodes, as well as the placement of these relays. However, finding an optimal solution by directly solving this complex problem is impractical due to its numerous constraints and interconnected nature. Therefore, we develop a distributed, iterative solution method, consisting of two main components: a distributed network coding scheme that enables a decentralized, efficient coding matrix selection for each user, and a concurrent optimization algorithm that simultaneously allocates relays and determines power levels. We show that our proposed method distributes network coding efficiently, reduces linearity, and conserves power while finding a suitable relay location. Results from a real-world network experiment confim that our method reduces energy consumption by 23.6% compared to a non-coding approach and, even more significantly, by 35.5% relative to a coding method that lacks linearity reduction and relay optimization.

Inning up on a $d$-wave superconductor's surface, a particular impurity known as Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) produces distinct, closely-spaced energy levels close to the Fermi level. The origin of these levels' precise positioning remains unclear. In this study, starting with a straightforward, relativistic framework for an impurity free of spin, the research discovered that YSR states near the Fermi level are formed by a combination of local Andreev states and low-transmission, quasi-local states caused by a slight difference between the impurity's $z$-coordinate and the surrounding electrons' effective $z$-coordinate. This discovery is then used to a more complex theory that incorporates spin-orbit interaction and relativistic orbital motion. The research found that both theories predict YSR states' splittings proportional to the superconductor's gap, as well as an unusual splitting for states produced by $k_x$ scattering in a particular $s$-wave superconductor. The research then explored the effects of magnetism in a particular YSR state produced by a manganese impurity on the Nb(110) surface. The magnetism caused a change in the impurity's effective $z$-coordinate, resulting in a particular YSR state that is not spin-polarized, as well as changes to several other YSR states produced by manganese dimers on the Nb(110) surface.
