Measuring inter-beat intervals provides essential information about a person's heart behavior, offering potential early warnings for heart diseases and more effective pain relief during activities like exercise. There are two main approaches to estimating inter-beat intervals from raw ECG signals: mathematical formulas and machine learning models. This paper evaluates a complex neural network known as Tiramisu and compares it to another complex model called U-Net. Additionally, it develops a simplified version of the Tiramisu model by subtracting some of its components and evaluates both the complex and simplified versions alongside four established methods. Testing these approaches with real heart signals yielded results showing the proposed models' accuracy, with the complex Tiramisu model achieving 99.685% accuracy, the simplified Tiramisu model achieving 99.672% accuracy, and six other methods having lower accuracy.

The applications of tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) have broadened into various domains such as multivariate data analysis and medical image processing. Recent advancements have led to the development of several Monte Carlo algorithms for calculating the t-SVD, each with distinct methodologies. Our approach builds upon the existing literature, drawing inspiration from a 2006 paper by Nielsen and Sorensen, to develop a flexible and efficient algorithm that applies the random matrix theory to the tensor decomposition problem. Our method is characterized by an increased likelihood of convergence in fewer iterations compared to other approaches. Furthermore, it allows for control over the number of iterations by adjusting the acceptable error threshold. Even in cases where the tensor is completely sampled from a random matrix, our algorithm is theoretically proven to produce results accurate to the 7th power of the number of iterations. Our study compares the performance of this algorithm to other existing methods, demonstrating its efficiency based on actual computations. An implementation of this algorithm, along with a accompanying demonstration, can be found on the TensorLy repository at https://github.com/tensornology/tensorly.

Real-world networks often exhibit dynamic properties, such as new connections forming and existing ones disappearing, either periodically or indefinitely. Various social media platforms, such as Twitter and Facebook, are examples of such ephemeral graphs, where a graph's structure and significance can significantly change over time. However, widely-used embedding techniques that focus on structural attributes overlook this temporal aspect. Our key objective is to create a unified framework for representing evolving graphs with an attention-based multi-task learning approach. Our model analyzes temporal patterns in these networks by considering the evolution of community-like structures over time. We conduct experiments on both artificially-designed and actual evolving graphs to demonstrate the efficacy of our method, with results showing improved node representation accuracy.

By constructing a two-body nuclear interaction and incorporating realistic three-body forces, researchers have computationally derived the binding energy of deuterium and its spectrum. Utilizing the variational method with a hyperspherical harmonic basis, the research simulated the quantum dynamics of the bound system, and a recent study has found the $^7$H ground state by introducing an unconventional two-body nuclear interaction that does not include the Pauli exclusion principle's corrections. This study has found the ground state of $^7$H as a $^3$H excitation of 4 neutrons without incorporating electromagnetic corrections in the theoretical framework. The research has a crucial implication for future experiments, as it suggests that $^7$H's binding energy is unlikely to be measured in existing experiments due to its distinct phase space distribution.

Research into the Nirenberg problem with a semilinear equation has concentrated on the maximal rigidity of this type of problem. A previous study demonstrated that when the boundary conditions are non-trivial, this type of equation exhibits non-trivial solutions, which has led researchers to investigate the Nirenberg problem with a linear restriction. Studies have shown that when the dimension is greater than eight, this problem has no non-trivial solutions, which highlights the complexity of this issue. A new study explores the Nirenberg issue on a truncated sequence of half spheres with a sequence of increasing radii, which shows that non-trivial solutions can occur for any dimension above eight. A sufficient condition has been established for the existence of these non-trivial solutions, which occurs when the mean curvature vector is negatively correlated with the nonlinear term in a given neighbourhood of a contact sphere in a half sphere.

This research introduces a novel learning method, called SINK, which utilizes the Sinkhorn distance in conjunction with a gradient descent approach to acquire a deep, optimal representation within a low-dimensional framework. By incorporating the triangle inequality property into the distance metric, where the initial and final representations, as well as an intermediate representation, are involved, the search space can be effectively restricted. Furthermore, the learnable intermediate representation enables a sequence of representations to be identified in an orderly manner. These advancements enable the creation of a range of challenging simulated datasets. Notably, the proposed method demonstrates significant performance improvements in several applications, such as dimensionality reduction, metric learning, and contractive neural networks, when compared to existing solutions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought attention to contact tracing as a crucial strategy for slowing down the disease's spread. As the outbreak continues to evolve in different parts of the world, various countries are implementing their contact tracing initiatives, often collaborating with local tracing organizations to enhance the efficacy of their programs. In this study, we analyze the contact tracing efforts in England, focusing on the role of local tracing collaborations in the success of their contact tracing programs. Our findings indicate that areas with multiple tracing collaborations were indeed more efficient in contact tracing, but interestingly, this did not always translate to lower infection rates. It is crucial for future research to uncover the factors contributing to the ineffectiveness of contact tracing in certain settings.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a complex task, which can be simplified by leveraging the data from Gaia DR2. We utilized this DR2 to establish the distance of Melotte 72, a young open star cluster in the constellation of Scorpius. We performed various procedures to guarantee the data reliability. The initial step entailed selecting only the highest quality DR2 data for the cluster stars and applying extinction corrections to the cluster's physical location. We then generated color-magnitude diagrams for Melotte 72 in the JD- V/HV plane and fitted them using a logistic function to establish the location, brightness, and spectral type of its turn-off and hot subgroups. We also used this data to calculate the cluster's age, distance, mass, and solar membership rate. The results show that Melotte 72 is approximately 2.0+/- 0.3 kpc away and has a suspected proper motion varying between different sources, with A.C.  =  -7.633+/- 0.3, D. = -8.726+/- 0.3 kms^-1, with the mass accounting for approximately 180 to 340 suns within a radius of 6.5 pc. We also used this data to calculate the cluster's age, with the red giant branch of Melotte 72 estimated at around 1.1+/- 0.2 kyr old. We also determined the location of its A

We analyze a first-order stochastic process that takes values in the integer grid
$\mathbb{Z}^{d}$. The process begins at point $0$, and its distribution is parameterized by
the size of the grid, $n$. We study the expected Betti numbers, which characterize the topological features
of the resulting partition. Our main finding involves deriving the limit points of these expected Betti numbers
as the dimension $d$ grows without bound and the step size goes to zero. We demonstrate that these limit points
relate to specific characteristics of the distribution with the step size as the probability measure. Next, we investigate
the statistical properties of these Betti numbers by computing their associated sample covariances.
Our results demonstrate that, for large dimensions, these sample covariances converge to specific matrices
whose entries depend on the characteristics of the distribution, with the step size as the correlation matrix.

Adjusting an eye-in-hand camera is crucial for successful pose estimation in robotics, but the process is often laborious and time-consuming due to the need for extensive calibration data, including multiple images and corresponding 3D point cloud information. Researchers previously relied on machine learning models trained on vast datasets, but these models require a significant amount of computational power and storage space, and are only effective within their trained parameters. In a breakthrough discovery, the authors propose an innovative method that enables the adjustment of an eye-in-hand camera solely using a 2D image, eliminating the need for expensive hardware like laser scanners and time-consuming annotations on collections of 3D scans. Their solution combines a trained image classifier, custom-made image processing tools, and the use of the environment's semantic features. In experiments conducted on a NVIDIA Jetson Nano, the authors demonstrate that their method outperforms state-of-the-art models, and is capable of real-time adjustment, outperforming the current fastest method by a factor of four.

In safety-critical domains, equipping agents with sound failure detection and response mechanisms is vital for ensuring their overall reliability. This paper reworks the CONDOR training framework, originally designed for developing robust agents in unstructured environments, to address failure modes triggered by agents' own mistakes. Within a constrained framework, CONDOR encourages agents to pinpoint and rectify errors, thereby expanding their skill set to include both corrective actions and predictive warning signs of impending failures. We extend this framework by introducing a new training objective that amplifies the importance of handling pre-existing faults, and test it across three complex environments characterized by high-dimensional states and unexplored state spaces. Our findings show that agents trained with this method achieve superior performance on both detecting and preventing faults.

The GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D map of the Milky Way region by tracking nearly a billion stars across the visible light spectrum and multiple photometric bands. As the most extensive sky survey to date, GAIA will offer scientists a vast number of opportunities to analyze the composition and structure of our local galaxy. The mission will create a homogeneous database with accurate star representations in 3D space, which will allow researchers to investigate various aspects of stellar development and galactic evolution. The scientific potential of GAIA has broad scope, encompassing topics like the galactic disk's chemical composition, the development of stellar clusters, the distribution of stellar masses, and the presence of distant stars and galaxies within the Milky Way's boundary.

Vertex cover and treewidth are closely related, with treewidth being able to be computed in polynomial time when a perfect vertex cover is given. A vertex cover is considered perfect if every vertex in the cover directly connects to every vertex outside of it. An equivalent data structure called a compact vertex cover (CVC) provides a perfect vertex cover and allows for efficient updating after vertex additions or removals, with operations such as vertex deletion taking O(n^(1/2 + ε)) time and vertex addition taking O(n^(1/2)) time, with ε being a constant greater than 0. (Chen et al., 2011) achieved these results using an auxiliary graph, with the main function of the structure being to facilitate treewidth computation after various changes. Treewidth computation time in (Chen et al., 2011) is polynomial, with the possibility of treewidth being 0. 

We have developed an improved version of the CVC, with the ability to perform certain operations in near-linear time, with the ability to achieve a perfect vertex cover, but with the ability to remove vertices in O(n^(1/2 + ε)) time, with the result that the function has a significant trade-off between update speed and time to find a perfect vertex cover. Due to this, we have developed an algorithm to compute treewidth after various changes, with the result that the treewidth can be computed in O(n^(1/2 + ε)) time, with the result

Most methods for analyzing network data assume a uniform approach to assigning nodes into groups, but our research reveals significant variations in responding to nodal characteristics. To address this, we propose a versatile family of weighting schemes tailored to create meaningful interactions between nodes or groups, applying these to synthetic and actual network data. Our results demonstrate that these weighting schemes can amplify the accuracy of existing methods for analyzing network patterns, as long as the input data accurately represents the network. Conversely, we found that these weighting schemes can impair analytical accuracy when the input data fails to accurately represent the network, regardless of its size. Moreover, we found that analyzing smaller networks, regardless of its size, does not guarantee accurate results and can even make analytical accuracy deteriorate as the network size increases. Our research also highlight the significance of examining the balance between within-group and between-group connections, which can influence the accuracy of analytical outcomes.

We introduce a novel method for estimating the uncertainty associated with predictions made by physics-informed neural networks. By incorporating a prior understanding of the relationship between input data and their corresponding outputs, we can adjust predictions to ensure they conform to known physical principles. Our approach allows for predictions to be confined within a predefined margin of uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a case involving heat equations, where we leverage known relationships between heat source strength and temperature to calibrate the neural network's confidence in its predictions. Furthermore, we observe that the optimized predictions achieved with our method surpass the accuracy of traditional physics-informed neural networks.

Epidemiological research utilizes various data sources to tackle numerous questions, and has recently benefited from the application of big data, encompassing not only traditional sources, but also inclusion of genetic data, spatial location information, and images. The same holds for computational techniques, where the integration of machine learning and artificial intelligence is increasingly essential. This transformation not only expands the scope of epidemiology but also alters its core, necessitating the incorporation of relevant methodologies from statistical learning, computer science, and statistics. This work examines current methodologies for addressing various epidemiological topics, and highlights future challenges, and outlines two specific applications of spatial analytics in epidemiology.

To differentiate the Majorana peak from other features in tunneling spectra, such as those produced by Andreev states, we suggest a method involving a tunneling junction with a high resistance (> 1 Ohm) made of a material that blocks charge transport. Such a resistance, being much larger than the Coulomb energy, has little impact on the system's behavior, but hinders the flow of charge by making the tunneling probability extremely low. This setup has the added benefit of simplifying spectra interpretation by eliminating non-uniformities in the system's density and reducing the appearance of peaks produced by Andreev states. Moreover, the high resistance barrier can be easily made in the form of a nanoscale strip or dot, thereby not significantly affecting the system's tunneling probability. This setup has the added benefit of simplifying spectra interpretation by eliminating non-uniformities in the system's density and reducing the appearance of peaks produced by Andreev states. This proposal has the advantage of simplifying experimental design while improving data interpretation.

Linear bandits, a type of contextual bandits, assume that context and action effects are linear, resulting in a well-defined model that predicts action rewards. While this model's generative aspect is frequently investigated, its predictive aspect is often overlooked, leading to unclear boundaries between identification and estimation in linear bandit models. This research tackles these ambiguities by presenting two main contributions. Firstly, it develops a theoretical framework for modeling diverse action sets in a bandit scenario with uniformly distributed actions, separating the identification of underlying parameters from the estimation of parameters within this setting. Secondly, it uses this constructed model to establish theoretical bounds between inference and estimation, accompanied by a proof-of-concept implementation of an information-theoretic inference method that yields competitive results in a simulated environment compared to other popular approaches.

Researchers have discovered that in graphene with gaps, the movement of charge carriers exhibits a directional flow, this effect being a result of a combination of the natural processes of gap formation and the spinning motion of electrons. By applying a specific type of magnetic field, the rotational motion of electrons within graphene can lead to its uniform movement in a predetermined pattern. A similar model was developed that explains how the spinning motion of electrons in graphene with holes contributes to their overall movement. Both situations demonstrate that the rotational motion of electrons produces a new type of uniform flow that is similar in nature to a specific kind of uniform flow associated with electrons in multi-layered materials, this new uniform flow being referred to as a uniform orbital flow. Since the uniform flow associated with electrons in multi-layered materials is caused by different states of electrons, this new uniform flow being referred to as a uniform orbital flow is caused by the different rotational motions of electrons. Additionally, based on the principle that the uniform flow associated with electrons in multi-layered materials is caused by different states of electrons, this new uniform flow being referred to as a uniform orbital flow can be referred to as a uniform Hall flow, the term 'Hall' implying that the uniform flow is caused by different states of electrons. Therefore, the uniform flow being referred to as a uniform orbital flow can also be referred to as a uniform Hall flow, the term 'Hall' implying that the uniform flow is caused by different states of electrons.

Machine learning models' effectiveness in the real world largely depends on their performance outside of the boundaries defined by the training data. However, the fact that machine learning models can be overly confident in their predictions when they're not supposed to be, poses a significant issue. Researchers have been focusing on the robustness of these models by investigating how they can be modified to withstand data manipulation. This paper proposes a new method that utilizes reinforcement learning to protect Graph Neural Networks against data corruption by introducing an optional channel for model outputs, which can be modified accordingly. The goal is to enhance model robustness by limiting the use of the optional channel through reinforcement learning optimization. Experimental results show that this method can significantly improve the resistance of models to corruption by transferring knowledge through the optional channel while reducing the impact of corrupted data.

The process of matching object catalogs involves identifying and linking objects between different catalogs based on their properties. This process is crucial for creating unified object lists and aligning the object's position and measurement values accurately. The step involves using cross-matching to compare objects at varying signal-to-noise ratios and photometric bands. By cross-matching, it's possible to assess the level of uncertainty or noise present for each object and determine the accuracy of its properties. By incorporating the information from all the object's properties into the cross-matching algorithm, it's possible to obtain a more reliable match compared to using a single parameter in isolation. The method is demonstrated to yield an overall matching precision of 94.7% and a resolution of mismatch of 5.1%, based on a small test sample of less than 1000 objects which is then expanded to include 10 million objects, resulting in the initial 94.7% accuracy expanding by only a fraction of a percent. The outcome shows that the technique provides a highly accurate and reliable match which is essentially unchanged when applied to large datasets.

In this paper, a minimal edge cover of an infinite hypergraph is a subset of its edges that intersects with all the hypergraph's edges, and we investigate a new measure of the hypergraph's size, $\ex^*$, based on the smallest minimal edge cover for countably infinite hypergraphs. It is also shown that this hypergraph size measure is equivalent to the largest possible size of a minimal edge cover and that both measures are equivalent to the infinity version of the hypergraph's dimension. The relation of the size measure $\ex^*$ to infinite hypergraph properties, such as colorability and bipartability, is then explored.

The continuous expansion of ontologies in diverse domains relies heavily on user-generated content, driving their steadily increasing popularity. Visualizations play a crucial role in facilitating domain expert contributions by showcasing specific aspects of an ontology. To address this, we have developed OntoPlot, a novel visualization designed to display relationships within an ontology. By comparing OntoPlot with existing method, particularly Camille, we have demonstrated its advantages using three real-world ontologies. Furthermore, a user study has shown that OntoPlot enhances user experience, leading to increased engagement and understanding of ontology content, ultimately paving the way for improved visualization contributions.

This research introduces an innovative approach to semi-supervised automatic speech recognition systems by leveraging unsupervised domain adaptation. The proposed method combines two key techniques: a cycle-consistent training method to facilitate cross-domain training, and a novel inter-domain penalty to maintain consistency between speech and transcript domains. Unlike previous methods, the proposed approach trains a single, unified network model for both speech and transcript generation without segregating the model into separate modules. As a result, the proposed system achieves significant reductions in unlabelled speech data requirements and yields significant performance improvements on the WSJ, LibriSpeech, and Voxforge datasets. For example, the system is able to attain a word error rate of 8.0% on the LibriSpeech test set using only 10% labeled data, a marked improvement over the 16.0% error rate achieved by the system using no unsupervised data.

A cognitive architecture grounded in active inference can facilitate robot navigation, but navigating through unfamiliar environments poses significant challenges, especially when using a basic framework. This work presents an innovative robot navigation method inspired by the active inference theory, in which the agent develops a detailed mind model closely reflecting its physical environment. We propose an innovative approach combining prior knowledge and sensor data, with a novel method for estimating uncertainty in the mind model. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in building a precise mind model of an environment and show that it compares favorably to established lapnet and deepRRT navigation techniques in both real-world and simulated conditions. Additionally, experiments reveal that the proposed method enables the agent to accurately predict the consequences of its movements, thereby reducing the uncertainty surrounding its mind model.

The Soret effect, which describes the separation of a binary mixture under a temperature gradient, is examined from a different perspective by considering the role of soft molecules with numerous internal degrees of freedom. These molecules, featuring multiple rotational and translational states, exhibit a broad range of freedom. In this context, the primary responsibility of these freedom degrees is to minimize the influence of internal movements on the collective movement of molecules, thus facilitating a smooth and continuous transition between different degrees of freedom as they adapt to the external temperature gradient. Consequently, the separation that occurs within the system, characterized by the relative movement of molecules, is directly related to the smooth transition of internal freedom degrees. Theoretical calculations of the Soret coefficient for the binary system based on the multi-freedom model reveal a strong correlation between the coefficient and the number of available freedom degrees, which increases approximately linearly. The resulting magnitude is proportional to the number of freedom degrees with a value greater than one. The Soret coefficient and separation within the system reach their maximum values at a specific temperature, which depends on the type of soft molecules and their composition, due to the contrasting behavior of different freedom degrees under varying temperature conditions. The freedom degrees with temperatures close to the transition point exhibit pronounced movement, while those at higher or lower temperatures remain relatively inactive. The separation within the system remains nearly zero above or below the critical temperature, except for a sharp increase around this point, which steadily declines with the extent of the temperature deviation from the critical value.

In the realm of music composition, both automated and human composers create musical pieces that deviate from established concepts of traditional music, leading to discussions on the societal implications of such works. This research explores how natural language processing techniques, specifically the application of transformer-based language models, can be utilized to evaluate musical compositions from a unique perspective. By analyzing both inherent and induced representations of a composed piece, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of transformer-based models in distinguishing intricate elements within contemporary music. The research also identifies potential limitations of these models in addressing various challenges associated with their training. Furthermore, this research develops innovative methods for resolving critical challenges in training these models on musical data, including inconsistent data formats and conflicting judgment aggregation methods.

This study addresses the challenge of reducing false positives in domain adaptation of pedestrian detection, and proposes the Superspacing Re-Ranking approach to achieve this goal. To begin, a siamese network extracts similarity features for a two-dimensional ranking of box predictions, and then a super-spaced loss function is utilized to maintain the relative order of predictions across different domains. Furthermore, the approach incorporates a hard example mining component to further improve performance. The evaluation of Superspacing Re-Ranking demonstrates a notable improvement in domain adaptation of pedestrian detection, with reductions of up to 52.5% and 12.6% in average precision at a false positive rate of 10 when compared to the Fast-RCNN baseline on the CityPersons and CityPersonsOC datasets, respectively.

This study presents an innovative method for revitalizing compromised audio
signals by leveraging techniques originally developed for image restoration and
digital waveform reconstruction. Existing audio restoration methods are
often confined to their underlying primary models or are heavily influenced by
them, thereby restricting the scope of applicable restoration methods. To
explore novel audio restoration techniques, we adopt a cross-domain approach,
along with an audio pre-processing mechanism that facilitates the seamless
transfer of information across different domains. Consequently, this enables
the adaptation of sophisticated image processing algorithms, originally unsuited
for audio, and combines their outcomes with the results of conventional audio
processing methods through refined synthesis algorithms. These synergistic
effects result in a substantial enhancement of the compromised audio quality.
To facilitate the comparison of our method with baseline models, we introduce
a novel framework that determines the similarity between audio signals by
measuring their mutual information under two distinct encoding schemes. Our
experiments with both synthetic and real-world audio samples demonstrate
superior results for our novel approach.

This study delves into the impact of a user's mistaken estimation of the release point for an object during a throwing motion. An earlier finding demonstrated that users can effectively replicate a given trajectory with an initial release point, but only if they initially new the release point.  This led to the development of a plan to investigate the opposite scenario, where users are given a trajectory but must determine the optimal release point to achieve the desired path.  The user's throwing technique in this scenario includes an error in estimating the release point, and we investigate how this initial mistake affects the resulting throwing motion.  Our method for finding the most suitable release point involves iteratively sampling potential release times from a uniform distribution and selecting the one that best aligns with the user's estimated throwing motion, and then using inverse kinematics to resolve the motion.  Our simulation data revealed that users who employed this technique could accurately reproduce throwing motions with varying release times.  However, when users were given a fixed release time and must determine the most suitable throwing motion to achieve the desired trajectory, significant errors occurred.  An experiment involving 32 participants showed that users who employed this technique resulted in a median distance between actual and intended impact points of 11.8 cm, whereas when given the release time and must adjust their throwing motion, the median distance of the impact points was 4.9 cm.  These results highlight the relative futility of using a method that optimizes the release time for a throwing motion, suggesting that

This research introduces an innovative decoding method that builds on the Sequence-to-Sequence framework by incorporating a tree-structured exploration space and leveraging syntactic connections. Conventional Sequence-to-Sequence models are restricted to linear search, whereas our approach allows for a flexible exploration of possible translations within a syntactically guided tree structure. By exploiting these syntactic connections, the proposed method can efficiently prune less promising translations. Experimental results derived from the Multi-Tree English-to-German translation dataset demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve comparable quality at a faster rate or outperform the baseline model. Additionally, the study analyzes decoding patterns and identifies characteristics that differ from the parent model, leading to questions about the optimal use of syntactic representations in Translation and Parsing tasks.

The formation of molecular complexes in space can serve as a model for understanding various physical and chemical processes that don't involve radiation. Two main factors - non-radiative processes and chemical reactions - enable the formation of molecular complexes in space. A tool has been developed to compare experimental and theoretical molecular bond strengths, specifically designed for understanding non-radiative processes in binary systems. The platform provides accurate binding energy data, allowing for a precise simulation of molecular complex distributions at different temperatures. A significant finding from our analysis is that traditional binding energy models often overestimate molecular complex stability. It's hoped the platform will facilitate discussions and spark new research in the fields of astrochemistry and ultracold chemistry. The data, accessible via a remote server, can also be utilized for predicting the destruction of molecular complexes through collisional processes.

In stochastic process modeling, a widely recognized technique involves mapping real-world phenomena onto probability distributions. However, there are instances where conventional approaches, centered on additive relationships, fall short of accurately replicating the underlying mechanisms. Recognizing the necessity of adapting distributions according to unique conditions or, better yet, developing algorithms that learn and adjust their parameters as data becomes available, can sometimes yield superior results. This study delves into the analysis and application of a multiplicative stochastic process, one that considers minimal variations, and explores its potential use in tasks such as estimation, prediction, and reliance assessment of systems on random events.

We explore the idea that an arbitrary $n$-qubit state $\rho$ is mixed (not pure) by examining how its expectation values for specific Pauli operators in certain measurement scenarios are calculated. By applying random Clifford circuits of a specific depth, we can create a set of measurable observables that converge quickly to a specific value, indicating the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the state $\rho$, which is directly related to its von Neumann entropy. This approach allows us to achieve convergence at a rate that is linear in the number of qubits, as opposed to the typically exponentially complex nature of the problem. This method is successfully applied to smaller random circuits consisting of up to 16 qubits and complex states mimicking real-world conditions with noise, where it accurately estimates key entropy values. This study opens the door for further research on entanglement assessment using shallow quantum circuits, which could lead to the development of new tools for studying complexity classes, notably $\mathcal{B}$.

We are studying the reflection of water waves generated by a target two-dimensional profile that decreases as time increases, in a basin of infinite depth where the water waves are periodic in the crosswise direction. This study considers the effect of waves whose frequencies are far apart and superimposed on one another. We show that the scattering theory approach can be used to translate this problem, which is difficult to solve numerically, into a new equation that is easier to analyze. We then demonstrate that the reflection coefficient for this new equation exhibits a distinct behavior as the frequency increases. It is also shown that the integration of this new equation over a specific range can provide the amount of energy that is being reflected. Although a precise, analytical solution to this integration is available only for certain waves, it is shown that the reflection coefficient remains nonzero as the frequency increases without bound for a specific class of waves, which was discovered by Zou and Wu in 2012. This new equation is used to solve a number of questions about the behavior of water waves, including how much energy is reflected and how this amount changes as the frequency increases.

To ensure the accuracy of machine learning models in real-world applications, it is crucial to evaluate their reliability after replacing key components. This requirement is particularly challenging when processing human-generated text like product reviews, which often contains missing or altered attributes. Existing text categorization models are not designed to handle such data variations. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique called Sibylvariant, which effectively represents text variations by assigning a special token, thus enabling traditional transformer-based models to accurately classify product reviews with attributes even when they are partially missing. Unlike previous solutions, Sibylvariant introduces a straightforward method by treating attribute variations as a subpopulation of the original population, preserving the original distribution. Through this approach, models can maintain consistency between training and testing phases. Our findings demonstrate that Sibylvariant improves RobustPreTrained Model (RPT) accuracy on a product review categorization benchmark by 10.0% or more. Additionally, with our method, a language model can accurately perform text categorization after replacing the previous method, achieving an enhanced accuracy of 4.0%.

In the realm of artificial intelligence, Meta-Learning continues to gain prominence as a subfield of learning systems. A Meta-Learning system, characterized as an 'intelligence that learns how to learn', seeks to expedite the process of system development by facilitating faster design and training for various tasks. Our focus lies in understanding the relationship between problem-solving challenges and the feasibility of learning these problems through adaptation. We define problem bin α and solution function f such that each input x corresponds to a unique output f(x) ∈ ℝ. The solution function f represents the target state for our learning system, meant to be acquired through minimal data collection and adaptation. Our studies, assuming limited and label-free data, aim to identify the minimal data required for feasible adaptation within a binary classification framework. Furthermore, we investigate the potential trade-offs between data requirements, computational complexity, and memory constraints. Our work lies at the intersection of theoretical and practical studies, aiming to establish a comprehensive understanding of feasible adaptation.

Building highly accurate neural machine translation models often depends on pre-trained language models, which can be expensive both in terms of computational resources and energy consumption. A recent study aims to create lightweight machine translation models by utilizing knowledge extraction techniques instead of model compression. This paper compares the stability of knowledge extraction and model compression in the context of multilingual neural machine translation. The experiment shows that model compression yields similar results with a significantly smaller model, whereas knowledge extraction produces accurate translations but proves unstable due to continuous changes in the vocabulary. Contrary to low-resource MT challenges, we argue that model compression, particularly quantization, is a more reliable approach for building lightweight NMT models.

We devise a hypergraph, denoted as $\mathcal{G}_0$, and a sequence of hypergraphs as $\mathcal{G}_i$, such that $\mathcal{G}_i$ is derived from $\mathcal{G}_{i-1}$ with the edge $e_{i-1}$ subdivising an existing edge $e_{\mathrm{old}}$ in $\mathcal{G}_{i-1}$. For every $i$, a modified Lagrangian density, denoted as $L_i$, is constructed and satisfies the Taylor condition; in turn, this leads to a planar embedding of the augmented hypergraph $\mathcal{G}_i$ with energy (or zeta function) equal to $L_i$. As a result, this process can be repeated an arbitrary number of times $k$, ultimately yielding a revised Lagrangian density, denoted as $L$, which is a product of the $k$ individual modifications and satisfies the Taylor condition; in turn, this leads to a planar embedding of the hypergraph $\mathcal{G}_0$ with energy (or zeta function) equal to $L$. This approach provides an efficient method for exactly solving a system of equations with matrices containing specific properties - a system that is equivalent to Duffin-Kleinert equations when restricted to certain matrices.

Accurate diagnosis of lung conditions, such as pneumonia, relies on radiology reports which are highly reliable but slow to produce, hence automating the analysis is of utmost importance. Pneumonia in X-rays is identified by the presence of opacities which can be detected through segmentation. Deep learning, particularly fully convolutional neural networks, has proven successful in segmentation tasks. However, deep learning models require substantial amounts of labeled data, thus hindering their application. This paper investigates whether generating synthetic labels using supervised learning on enhanced images, such as with a UNet model, can provide a comparable or better solution than the traditional method, using augmented synthetic data, for a pneumonia segmentation task, also using augmented synthetic data. We found that combining both approaches produced the best results, with the minority class (background) performing better than the majority (pneumonia), showcasing the task's complexity.

While fine-grained image description skills are highly valued in the field,
these abilities often conflict with the requirement for neutral descriptions.
To address this challenge, we develop a versatile approach that enables
fine-grained description models to be adapted for diverse perspectives,
including those based on biases and pre-existing assumptions.
Our proposed framework incorporates a flexible prompt system,
enabling the description skill to be modified with ease.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by improving
state-of-the-art description models and neutralization techniques,
and show that it facilitates an efficient and robust description capability
that can be replicated with fewer parameters than the original model.

This research explores non-deterministic influence, examining the concept of causation in the context of changes that affect game state outcomes. We establish a framework for evaluating causal relationships using decision trees, define relevant notions within this context (such as non-anticipating conditions, impact, and efficacy), and provide equivalent formulations to established concepts (such as the counterfactual reasoner's view of causation and optimal action). We then apply this framework to the game of Cactus, focusing on the initial step where a player chooses to plant it or not. Our definitions and equivalences relate the game's causality to concepts from philosophical reasoning, demonstrating that a player's decision to plant the Cactus is the cause of its subsequent state only if it meets specific conditions, and that this analysis sheds light on the principles of inductive reasoning.

Deep learning training has seen significant advancements, yet researchers continue to grapple with two pressing issues: adapting complex, layer-rich models to simpler problems and scaling these models up efficiently. A new technique known as adaptive deep learning has emerged as a potential solution, allowing for the seamless adaptation of models by modifying individual layers instead of the entire network's parameters. Additionally, this approach can be combined with distributed training to quickly and efficiently scale up models. This paper introduces the first complete adaptable and distributable deep learning system, fully realizing the potential of adaptive deep learning, while showcasing the results of several experimental studies that highlight the technique's benefits, including dramatic improvements in model scalability, memory efficiency, and parameter optimization.

Voice translation technology allows people to learn a single skill that can be used 
in any language, allowing those with disabilities to participate in future 
multilingual communities through accessible education. Our research focuses on 
developing zero-shot voice translation that doesn't require retraining. We've 
proposed two key advancements: first, creating a universal acoustic model that 
can translate any source language into any target language without needing 
retraining, and second, designing a language representation model that can perform 
translation without the need for mid-result features to be stored. Our model 
outperforms previous models in both English-Persian and English-Hindi translations, 
beating the average of previous results and also improving translation results in 
terms of computational efficiency.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, incorporating boundary conditions that dynamically change in line with the temperature gradient. The investigation commences with an examination of the general mathematical properties inherent to the heat conduction equation, encompassing both standard internal sources and boundary-related sources, thereby ensuring its continuity within the study domain. There are two primary scenarios being explored. Firstly, the well-established internal heat conduction theory is applied, resulting in the derivation of a dynamic boundary condition. Secondly, the impact of dynamic boundary conditions on the thermal regime is evaluated, leading to the derivation of a dynamic boundary condition for the heat equation. Ultimately, the variation of parameters in both instances is analyzed, and corresponding solutions are rigorously proven by means of a compact vector-valued operator approach, thereby providing concrete insight into the general behavior of thermoregulatory systems, as well as a thorough characterization of the long-term asymptotic behavior of such systems.

Precise energy generation and consumption forecasting is critical to operating a low-voltage electricity network efficiently, yet it remains a complex challenge due to the highly variable and unpredictable nature of energy production from renewable energy sources, as well as changes in consumer behavior and energy usage patterns. We investigated the potential benefits of fusing probabilistic forecasts to enhance the accuracy and reliability of energy load prediction, using the ESM2020 dataset that outlines load forecasts for a Dutch low-voltage electricity district, and found that combining forecasts can lead to a significant improvement in forecasting accuracy, with the best results achieved through the fusion of two forecasts produced by different models, resulting in a Charles Foster-type model that exhibits a MAE of 0.032 MW and a CCI of 0.996, demonstrating great promise for the practical application of this approach in real-world load prediction scenarios.

Deep learning's remarkable achievements have sparked widespread interest in
automating machine learning model development. This surge in interest has led to
the emergence of Automated Machine Learning, a subfield focused on automating
both the development and implementation of machine learning models. Despite the
advances in Automated Machine Learning, creating a machine learning model is still
a complex process for non-technical users. To bridge this gap, a new concept
called Digital Twin Machine Learning integrates digital twins with Automated
Machine Learning, enabling end-users to specify high-level requirements for a
model instead of getting lost in technical details. Digital Twin Machine Learning
allows users to define objectives such as data sources, relationships between
variables, and performance requirements, enabling a digital service to create a
custom model that aligns with their needs. Our system uses an interface with a
digital twin to gather information about the user's data and performance goals,
enabling it to provide a compatible model and configure the necessary
parameters. We showcase the effectiveness of our Digital Twin Machine Learning
framework through two real-world use cases, demonstrating its potential to create
innovative and effective machine learning models.

The availability of COVID-19 chest CT scans reliant on patient movement has led to a complex issue of accounting for uncertainty in COVID-19 lesion annotation. Current methods assume perfect annotations, but these have inaccuracies similar to those found in fully annotated scans. This results in localized lesions shifting farther away from their true positions, ultimately hindering model performance. In contrast, the benefits of semi-supervised approaches have been well-documented but their full potential for reducing uncertainty remains unclear. This study combines the ideas of weakly supervised learning for lesion detection and semi-supervised learning for reducing coordination uncertainty to outperform previous methods. The proposed framework uses label distribution matching to correct classification and lesion location errors, and semi-supervised learning to refine a CT segmentation model. This method achieves significant performance gains on a COVID-19 CT dataset using semi-supervised chest radiography for reducing coordination uncertainty.

A crucial component of spine radiology analysis is the accurate identification of vertebras, essential for a range of quantitative markers, such as bone mineral density. The task of vertebral identification from unoptimized 3D spine CT scans is challenging, causing a great deal of variation in accuracy among different techniques. The goal of this research paper is to develop a reliable and precise method to locate and recognize vertebras in CT scans with an unoptimized spinal column. The proposed method includes a new technique to align the spine and match the vertebras through an optimization process, taking into account the variation in spinal morphology. The method was tested using data from 50 subjects, applying manual identification of vertebras as a reference point. The results showed that the proposed method significantly outperformed existing methods of vertebral identification, resulting in a significant improvement in precision and overall performance. The source code for this methodology has been made available on GitHub, facilitating potential improvements by providing a clear explanation of the method's execution.

In systems with ultrastrong light coupling, vacuum fields exhibit distinct, non-peturbative behavior characterized by Rabi oscillations, which can give rise to various novel phenomena. A theoretical study explores the dynamics of a resonant electron interaction with a cavity under these conditions, focusing on the electron's dispersion relation and behavior within a two-dimensional cavity. It is demonstrated that a specific configuration of cavity dimensions and electron velocity can stabilize the electron's energy using vacuum oscillations, which might be generated by the cavity's resonance with the electron's internal structure. This stabilization mechanism could be realized in experiments involving materials with strong electron-photon interactions, such as graphene and nanomechanical single-photon emitters, which would allow for the precise measurement of graphene's band structure.

In the field of robotics, quadruped robots that utilize elastic actuators for movement are gaining more attention because these actuators allow the integration of multiple advantages, including reduced weight, increased noise resistance, improved tolerance to malfunction, and more energy-efficient operations. However, elastic actuators have a non-linear characteristic that can make it challenging for trajectory planning. This study aims to find a solution to this issue by introducing a novel method for quadruped movement control that enables the simulation of traditional in-flight dynamics using elastic actuators. By making this simulation possible, the proposed approach also offers an alternative for choosing suitable actuator elastic constants. We experimented with this new method on a small robotic quadruped device called the "Riva" built by researchers at the Czech Technical University in Prague, and the results showed that the proposed movement control has the potential to replace existing traditional in-flight dynamics methods in practical applications, including specific gait patterns and trajectories that include elastic movements in the legs.

The fundamental problem of quantum distinguishability has been revisited under two separate measurement conditions. Firstly, our analysis established a lower bound on the approximate probability of categorizing mixed quantum states $\rho_A$ and $\rho_B, using a positive operator-measurement scheme. This lower bound was found to be $\text{Tr}[\mathcal{B}(\rho_A,\rho_B)]^2$ and, in many instances, is achieved with a specific variational quantum distinguishability meter. Secondly, we explored the situation where both states are subjected to projective measurement in a specific basis. By utilizing the trace norm, we established a lower bound on the approximate probability of distinguishing $\rho_A$ and $\rho_B$. This lower bound was found to be $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^d \text{Tr}[\mathcal{B}(\rho_A,\rho_B^{(k)})]^2$ and, in many instances, is achieved with a specific simple meter.

The lower solar atmosphere's complex physics involves intricate processes such as heating, absorption, spicules, and mass ejections from the photosphere to thousands of km high in just a few minutes. These events are thought to be driven by MHD instabilities. The role of nanogiant cells, formed by the interaction of helical magnetic structures, in channeling tidal forces and facilitating tearing has been explored previously. This study examines the dynamics of tearing instability in a collisionless slab plasma at the Kyushu University Solar Center. The simulation shows that even in the absence of resistivity, waves generated by the instability can turn into nonlinear structures, developing the characteristics of X-points. The instability develops more rapidly along the open magnetic fields than along the closed fields, driven by Kelvin-Helmholtz-like forces, where the shear at the boundary of the open and closed fields acts as a critical factor. The growth of the instability is not simply a direct result of the helical nature of the magnetic fields, but rather depends on the local properties of the open and closed fields. The initial stages of the tearing instability take significantly less time than predicted by linear theory, and the formation of X-points occurs almost instantly in a collisionless environment. The next objective is to observe this process in 3D simulations, where initial results indicate that even small-scale X-points can rapidly give rise to helical structures. This study explores the utilization of artificial attribute control, known as fashion attribute manipulation, in the retrieval task. In the realm of fashion and computer vision, the primary focus has been on utilizing vast amounts of data to learn distinct features, only to have them subsequently discarded during the generation process. Our proposed method, an innovative attribute manipulation approach, instead relies on a unique architecture that preserves these features and achieves a considerable enhancement in performance. Notably, our method has been successfully demonstrated on a fashion retrieval task, even when only partially supervised. Additionally, our technique allows for better control over fashion attributes, thereby empowering the retrieval system with greater semantic understanding. We have meticulously documented our findings in a peer-reviewed paper and all associated code will be publicly accessible upon the paper's acceptance.

The main aim of this study is to investigate the use of dual gradient descent as a method for solving the general form of underdetermined linear problems in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. By applying a stopping rule based on the non-linear convergence theory developed by Kamran and Neubauer, we establish the convergence of dual gradient descent for recovering the exact solution of the underlying equation within any arbitrarily small margin of error. Furthermore, we provide practical implementation guidelines for dual gradient descent within the context of regularization problems in infinite-dimensional settings.

An essential component of a light field, the expense map, determines the amount of light present on a given point, taking into consideration the effects of distortion and occlusion from surrounding points. Existing methods for creating expense maps have shortcomings, particularly in the presence of occlusion from off-axis points. As a result, they often fail to accurately recover clear objects hidden from the view but visible from other angles. In response to this, we introduce the Occlusion-Aware Expense Creator (OCC), a novel approach for generating sample-based expense maps that accurately account for occlusion. By modeling the effects of each contributing ray, our approach considers both the coherence of anchor rays and the opacity of visible ones to produce more accurate results. By integrating these principles, our approach, compared to state-of-the-art methods, yields a significant improvement in estimated depths, especially in scenes where occlusion occurs, as demonstrated on public datasets.

This study leverages the bilinear method to derive the Fokas-Lenells equations' initialisation procedures for both rational and hyperbolic systems. Key representations of solutions are also obtained through the resulting gauge transformations. Notably, our derived formulas complement existing ones from a different approach by Merola, Omodei and Tamborella.

Effective actions for gravitational phenomena with non-Lorentz invariance can be derived in a straightforward manner using double field theory. This approach allows for a simple expression of the effective action in terms of the absolute four-volume, where the well-known general relativity action with a topological term is a special case. Specifically, we explore actions for gravity within a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, which have been discussed in the literature. By employing a specific gauge, the double field theory formalism helps to stabilize the scalar degree of freedom and yields an action whose scalar component mirrors the Schwarzschild-de Sitter solution's scalar component. Furthermore, we examine how this solution's properties can be derived from an AdS/CFT correspondence with a specific conformal symmetry.

To optimize the performance of IEEE 802.11 home networks, we suggest selecting the most suitable technology (a or v) for each device based on its geographical location. This would require the deployment of additional equipment, such as load sensors, to measure traffic on 802.11 channels. Using these sensors, a centralized controller can determine the most efficient technology for each device, thus improving the network's overall quality of service. This method can be implemented using existing 802.11k/v standards without requiring any further enhancements. We studied three scenarios: choosing between a and v in dual-subnet configurations, and using a or v in single-subnet configurations with or without the extension bridge mode. Our analysis demonstrates that, in dual-subnet setups with a, moving the device to a different subnet can lead to better performance, as it allows the device to use a different technology (channel) if its traffic load changes. In single-subnet setups with a, using the extension bridge mode (v) may yield better results, especially if the device is closer to the access point, as this would allow the device to use a different technology (channel) if its traffic load changes.
